speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether, in view of the comment of the Minister of Finance last evening that he saw very little chance of success at the present time of a program of voluntary price and wage restraints, and thereby seemed to pull the rug from under the Prices and Incomes Commission's program, is it the intention of the government to ask the commission to consider some other approach to the problem of inflation?

subsubtopic: INFLATION-VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS- INQUIRY AS TO OTHER MEASURES

They did not put all their hopes in the proposed December conference but are considering other techniques. Therefore, we remain optimistic and, I must say, very determined to continue the fight against inflation by every means available to the government.

speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The House resumed, from Monday, October 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Jack Cullen for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stanfield (p. 34).

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two sentences in the Speech from the Throne which state a principle with which I am in very strong agreement. I would be very happy if I could be convinced that the government also believes in this principle to the point of acting on it. The sentences are to be found at page 3 of Hansard for October 23, 1969, where the throne speech is reprinted. These are the sentences:
In addition to solving her Immediate problems, Canada must be prepared to face the coming challenges of the post industrial era. This calls for a systematic appraisal of Canadian society and of the basic principles that are to guide it.
As I understand those sentences, they say to us that we must solve our immediate problems but that we must solve them on the basis of principles that will be good in the years and the decades that lie ahead. I thoroughly and very strongly agree. One of the chief complaints my colleagues and I level at the present government is that it is not using methods to solve today's problems that will suffice in the years that lie ahead. Surely we are all agreed that the major problem facing us in Canada is poverty. Formerly we used the phrase "poverty in the midst of plenty". I think what is disturbing our society today is poverty in the midst of affluence. Anyone who would presume to understand and explain all the troubles which beset our day and generation, particularly by any simple answer, would be foolish. I think it is fair to say, however, that one of the reasons there is so much unrest and unhappiness, and one of the reasons there is so much resort to violence and other ways to try to correct things, is that far too many people are poor in the midst of a society and in the midst of an age in which they are given pictures of the kind of life they could enjoy but which they are completely denied.
Poverty in the midst of affluence is sapping the spirit of far too many of our people. In a moment or two, I shall document the statement I now make, that one of the main things that is wrong today is that the gap between the poor and the rich has widened immeasurably. It has become far too wide for our society to hold together. One thing we must do is narrow that gap. We must really take steps to bring up the standard of living of those in the lower brackets rather than just go on adding to the number of those who enjoy being part
DEBATES	169
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles of a wage or salary elite. In other words, I insist that an attack on poverty, an attack that is determined to get rid of it, an attack that it is determined to take us into the kind of day when we will not be forever talking about the poor, about the needy and about welfare cases, is what our government, our parliament and our country should be carrying out.
It is my contention that this government is: talking about poverty and talking about its concern for the poor, the pensioners and so on, but really is not applying itself to this problem, to use its own concept in the Speech from the Throne, by following principles that will be any good ten, 20 or 30 years from now. As I see it, our society in this age of affluence, and this age of technological capacities that are beyond our imagination, will hold together only if people enjoy as a matter of right their share of the standard of living we are able to produce. The phrase "guaranteed annual income" is one that is kicked around. The idea that people should enjoy a standard of living as of right is one that is becoming more and more part of the language of those who talk about these problems. But the government still talks about doing things for the needy and the poor when its job should be to create the kind of society and economy in which there are no poor.
The government says it is concerned about these matters and is showing its concern by an all-out war on inflation. Last night we listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) as he beat his breast and told us how the government is fighting inflation. Why, says the minister, are we fighting inflation; it is because we want to protect the pensions of the pensioners and the position of the poor. If I were to use the sophisticated language my friend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) sometimes uses I would just say "nuts". This is not a war on inflation that is designed to protect the poor or the pensioners because prices are still going up; the cost of living is rising faster than the pensions, and the pensioners and others who are on fixed incomes are losing their standard of living and will continue to lose it no matter what this government does. The government is using the old age pensioners and those on fixed incomes as an excuse for the kind of campaign that will keep inflation within bounds for the benefit of those at the upper levels.
As the Minister of Finance said last night, those who are strong, those who are in the
October 28. 1969

The Address-Mr. S. Knowles upper brackets, feel somehow they will keep up with it. As a matter of fact, some people gain because of inflation. All those people do not want is for it to get out of hand. So, we have this talk of needing to protect the pensioners to give us a so-called program against inflation which is really just a case of trying to protect those at the top of the scale.
I congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for joining some of the rest of us in complaining about the 2 per cent ceiling on the increase made in the old age pension and in the Canada Pension Plan benefit in any one year. Some of us have been complaining about this since it was brought into effect in 1966. But the Leader of the Opposition is perfectly right when he puts to the Minister of Finance a question which the Minister of Finance will not answer, namely, "Is this what you have to do; do you have to depress the position of the old age pensioners in order to fight inflation?"
The position of the pensioners is not improved by having the worth of their pensions devaluated. All it does is make it possible for those who are strong, organizations like the steel companies, to strengthen their position. But those at the bottom end of the stick are not covered at all. The government says-and we heard it again last night from the Minister of Finance-that this government has done so much for the old age pensioners. He started to tell us how there was an increase from $55 to $65 and to $75 and that now those on the guaranteed income supplement are up to $105 or $109 a month. This all sounds very good. But may I point out that the gap-and this is the important thing in social terms-between the pensions of our old age pensioners and our retired civil servants, on the one hand, and those of us, on the other hand, who are on incomes that we can bargain for, or the gap between pensioners and those working, has become so much wider that this increase the government talks about really does not mean anything at all.
[DOT] (12 noon)
Let me mention a case. It will not be very popular within these walls but I shall mention it anyway. The Minister of Finance likes to talk about the pension having gone up. Yes, it has. Twenty years ago it was $40 a month. Now, if one is receiving the GIS he can get about $109 a month, an increase of $69. That sounds good. But in that same period when the pension was $40 a month-and I refer to ourselves because we are typical of what has happened in Canadian society-we were receiving a total income of $6,000 a year. We are

now getting a total of $18,000. I point out that it is not just a matter of proportions, of one having gone up two and a half times and the other having gone up three times, but it is a matter of a greatly widened gap. The gap then was between $480 a year and $6,000; now the gap is between about $1,000 and $18,000. So, let the minister not stand there and beat his breast and tell us of the wonderful things the government has done for old age pensioners. In relative terms, in terms of the gap between them and society generally, the picture for them has become far worse.
I have on my desk a copy of a book called "Taxation Statistics", the 1969 edition, as published by the Department of National Revenue. As hon. members know, we get this book every year. It is full of figures which most of us have difficulty comprehending, and I am included in that group. But I am interested in a table on page 147 of this volume which is entitled, "Yearly Distribution of Taxable Returns by Income". It gives a certain amount of information for the years from 1946 to 1967. It tells how many people were reporting incomes in certain brackets for each of those years. Although those with incomes so low they are not reported are not included, I find that in 1946 there were one and a half million people reporting incomes of under $2,000, and 21 years later one and a half million is still the number of persons reporting incomes of under $3,000. So the position of those at the bottom of the income ladder has improved. In 21 years it has improved from $2,000 a year to $3,000 a year, but at the other end of the scale I find that whereas in 1946 there were only 20,000 taxpayers reporting incomes of over $10,000 a year, there are now 500,000 reporting such incomes.
I know that a case could be made on the other side by those of the chamber of commerce mentality who might say: "Look how we have improved things". That is fine. I am glad to know there are many more people receiving incomes on which they can enjoy the good and just life, and all the other kinds of lives of which mention is made. But while we have moved people of the middle and upper income brackets up to incomes that are in the stratosphere, we have still a million and a half of our people who report their incomes down at $3,000 a year or less. I submit that $3,000 a year in 1967 is less than was $2,000 in 1946.
The point I am making by these figures, and I make it in terms of relating old age pensions to other incomes, is that we have allowed the gap to widen in this country in
October 28, 1969

the last 20 years. Perhaps the thing has been happening since the beginning of time, but that is no reason for us not to stop it. So long as that situation continues to exist, I say our society is in danger of falling apart and that many of the things that happen today, many of the attempts to change things in ways that are not orthodox, many of the revolts and much of the unhappiness, are due to the fact that people live in the kind of age in which they learn over radio and television, as well as in feature magazines, of an affluent and luxurious life that is available but they cannot get anywhere near it because they are still in this depressed condition down at the bottom of the ladder.
It is very much like the picture in world terms. We have done much in the last couple of decades in terms of external aid. We have given tremendous sums of money in one way or another to the developing countries, and the living standards in the developing countries have been raised. However, at the same time we have raised our own average standards in North American and in the western world to such an extent that the gap between those in the developing countries and ourselves is wider than ever. I submit that that fact is one that challenges the world, and that unless something is done about it we are in for trouble. That is another subject that some of us talk about on other occasions. I believe that our government is terribly remiss in not yet having gone up even to the 1 per cent of our gross national product for external aid to which it is committed. I think it should be at least 2 per cent. But at this particular time I am talking about Canada. I think that the most serious problem facing us is the one that I have been trying to delineate, namely that we are allowing the gap between the poor and the wealthy to get wider than ever, that this is unfair to the poor and the needy and that it is dangerous so far as our society as a whole is concerned.
I know that it is very popular to talk about these things and to say that we must do something for the poor, but this is what bothers me about it. We keep on talking about doing things for the poor, but we still leave them out there, a different group who shall always be with us. Even if someone tries to quote the Bible at me, I do not agree that they need always be with us. In my view, what we have to do is to narrow this gap even if it means getting over the notion that it can be done without affecting the rest of us. This is what most people want to do. I think

The Address-Mr. S. Knowles the hon. member for York North (Mr. Dan-son) made an allusion to this yesterday, and I congratulate him on it. He said that we want to help the poor but we do not want it to cost us anything. I think there are ways in which we could bring the lower income people up to a certain level without having to cut into the incomes of those in the middle and upper brackets. I think that increasing employment, producing more goods and services-particularly the goods and services that the needy and the pensioners require-is one way to do it. However, I want to say categorically, even if I am speaking only for myself, that if we have only so much money to spend, if we have to follow this government line with which I do not agree, then we will have to re-allocate some of that money. We will have to impose higher taxes on high salaries and incomes, and on corporate wealth, so that we can increase the pensions of our old age pensioners and retired civil servants, so that we can give a better break to our war veterans, particularly those on the war veterans allowance.
Having made that reference, may I say that one of the things in the Woods report which pleased me in principle as well as because of the people who are affected-and incidentally this is something that the government has accepted in its white paper-is the recommendation that in the case of all Hong Kong veterans who can demonstrate any disability whatsoever, a 50 per cent disability pension will be awarded, which has the consequence of a full widow's pension when any of those veterans die. Actually, we learned in the Veterans Affairs Committee that this provision will cover just about all living Hong Kong veterans. I believe there are only about eight who have not established some disability and the whereabouts of some of them are beyond discovery. In spirit, therefore, what that report recommends is that those men who served in Hong Kong shall be treated as veterans virtually because they were there. Virtually because they went through the experience of those years as prisoners, they should be regarded as deserving of a 50 per cent disability pension, and their widows of a full widow's pension as a matter of right. It is a kind of guaranteed income.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
I like the idea, and we will have to come to the day when we do this across the board; when we stop talking about giving money to people because they are poor, because they
172	COMMONS DEBATES	October 28, 1969
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles
can meet a means or a needs test. We will have to reach the point where we say to people, "You are people; you are citizens; you are human beings. You are here as part of this modern industrial society, or post-industrial society, that can produce all kinds of wealth, and therefore you are entitled to a standard of living that is a reasonable minimum-yes, whether or not you do anything at all for it." I think this is implied in those two sentences I read at the start of my speech in which the government says that we have to make "a systematic appraisal of Canadian society and of the basic principles that are to guide it."
We will not build a new Canada or a just society for the year 2000 if in the year 2000 we are still saying, "We will give you a pension or an allowance if you are poor, if you can demonstrate that you need it." We won't hold this society together that long in that way. We will hold it together only if we achieve that equality among Canadians that says, "Because you are here, because you are Canadian, you have rights."
That is the reason that I make no apology whatsoever, even on the morning after that intemperate speech which we heard last night from the Minister of Finance, and even in the light of the things said in this House earlier this morning, for saying that what should be done right now by the government is to increase a number of these pensions about which some of us talk frequently.
The old age security pension should go up not just $1.58 a month in January; it should go up to $125 or $150 a month. The retired civil servants should have their pensions increased. In that connection, I welcome the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) and the speeches that have been made from time to time by other members of the House. These pensions should be raised in the order of 50 per cent or 60 per cent, without any question. I think that the principle which is to apply to the Hong Kong veterans might also apply to all World War I veterans still living, and their widows. Let us get away from these tests that can be applied. Let us say to people, "You belong to certain groups and you have rights." The day will come when everybody who is a Canadian has certain rights, particularly the right to a guaranteed standard of living, regardless of all other considerations.
I also think, Mr. Speaker, that something should be done about the case of those provinces which have not yet moved over to the

Canada Assistance Plan where people are still on old age assistance, or in receipt of the blind person's allowance or the disabled person's allowance. Those allowances should be increased. We left them behind when we last increased the old age security pension. Previously, when we used to increase the old age security pension we used to increase those other pensions as well. Now, we have brought these disability pensions up to $75 a month, but there is no guaranteed income supplement for these people.
All of these categories should receive pension increases right now. For the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance to say, "We cannot afford to do this because we have an austerity program and we have to fight inflation" is, I think, sheer nonsense. In fact, I think I am entitled to use the word hypocrisy, because it does not solve the problems of pensioners at all to carry on this phony war against inflation. Their position is getting worse by the month and by the week.
In my view we could afford pension increases on the basis of increased employment. I think that is the way to do it. But if the government is not prepared for that and does not have the wit to devise policies that will result in increased employment, and if it says, "We have only so much money to go around," then I say do not ask the pensioners to bear the brunt of the fight against inflation.
If members of the government say they feel for pensioners, then let the government help them out right now. If that means increasing taxes at the higher income levels I am for it. If that means cutting out some of the wasteful, extravagant expenditures such as those on the Prime Minister's staff, then I am for that, too. In fact, I am sure that all governmental expenditures, as with expenditures of society as a whole, have all kinds of fat at the top, with all kinds of affluence being enjoyed by do-gooders who are concerned about the poor provided this concern does not cost them a cent, provided it does not mean a lessening of their privileged position.
I do not think this is the kind of society that will hold together, the kind of society that is satisfied to leave one and a half million people in the position that they report incomes of less than $3,000 a year, while we go on trying to put as many people as we can into a wage and salary elite. To me this is extremely important, not just because of the needs that these people face right now, but it is extremely important if we are to hold our society together.
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
So, Mr. Speaker, I say that I welcome this declaration of principle that the government has given us in the Speech from the Throne, its assertion that we have to solve today's problems in the light of basic principles that will guide us in the years that lie ahead. But I ask this question: Does anybody in this House of Commons think we are going to guide our society ten or 20 years from now on the basis of means tests and needs tests, on the basis of keeping thousands, perhaps millions of our people down in lower brackets while others are away up in the stratosphere?
Surely, the only principle that is going to hold our economy, our society and our people together is one which makes the declaration that we are all Canadians and we are all entitled to a certain share of the wealth we are able to produce. That means a guaranteed minimum income below which no one will be allowed to fall. That means people enjoying and having that income as a matter of right. It means getting away from the day when the best the government can do is to say to people, "We will help out and fight battles for you if you are poor." Let us stop using that language. Let us not divide ourselves between the rich and the poor. Let us all be humans. Let us all be Canadians. Let us devise policies that will make things better for Canadians now, and better for Canadians in the future.
A clear demonstration that the government believes in the two sentences that I quoted at the beginning of my remarks would be given if the government would say, "All right; right now, as a matter of right we will say to the old age pensioners, we will say to the retired civil servants, we will say to the veterans on the veterans allowance, we will say to other pensioners, 'Even though there is an austerity situation, even though there are problems you have rights. We are going to accord those rights to you by increasing your pensions, and we believe that having done so things will be better both for you and for the country as a whole.' "
If the government would respond to the plea that some of us in this House have been making across the years, and give the pension increases we have been urging, it would be a better day for our older people now, and a much better day for all our people in the Canada of the future.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to congratulate the mover and

The Address-Mr. Godin the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. members for Sarnia and Lapointe (Messrs. Cullen and Marceau). They performed admirably, speaking with remarkable ease in either of the two official languages.
I have great admiration for them in that respect. As for myself, I am not outstanding in that field, but I hope that someday I shall be able to speak a second language. Unfortunately, I have little time for practice now because t he riding I have the honour of representing includes 90,000 people.
On the other hand, it is obvious that the four members from Prince Edward Island who represent 105,000 constituents are in a better position than I to become bilingual, if they devote their spare time to study.
Mr. Speaker, let us leave for a moment the individual ridings to consider the country as a whole. The Speech from the Throne of Thursday last contains many amendments to the just society proposed a year ago, and the numerous questions we shall have to deal with this year are evidence that last year's legislation has to be done again.
Although we intend to deal with all questions and to amend several laws, we may rightly question the results, in view of the fact that Canadians are still squeezed between a large national output, on the one hand, and accumulated surpluses as well as inadequate purchasing power, on the other hand. In order to divert people's attention, economists contradict themselves publicly about the causes of poverty in an affluent society.
Those quite knowledgeable men, and others who are less knowledgeable as well, take pleasure in classifying objectives of economic behaviour, as they say so well, in the hope of palliating structural and regional disparities and distortions. Everything is allowed to cover up the real truth and to hide from the people the true reasons for the period of unrest we are going through.
For instance, we refer to the chronic period of unemployment Canada has been experiencing for a few years as the cyclic and seasonal fluctuations of employment.
While financing charges and various taxes push upwards the prices of commodities and services essential to our survival, the people responsible for those increases tell us of plans to stabilize prices at a reasonable level.
While computers take the place of accountants and clerical workers, while machines take over from the workers in the plants, we

October 28, 1969
The Address-Mr. Godin still unfortunately find within the Canadian administration some dreamers who say that full employment is still possible.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tries his hand at changing the meaning of words to justify his inaction with regard to the real issues and to be able to launch a mixed attack on problems that do not exist. In my opinion, the most misused word in Canada, the word that does for everything, is "inflation".
Here, I would like to refer to page 2 of Hansard, for October 23, where the following can be found:
There are many obstacles to be overcome if we are to achieve our economic goals, but inflation is undoubtedly the most serious and the most difficult to control.
Mr. Speaker, the word "inflation" was really representative of the situation that prevailed during the war and the following years.
In fact, as most workers were then paid to destroy or to make articles intended for destruction, what was bound to happen happened. At one time there was more money in the citizens' pockets. The purchasing power was stronger, higher than the value of the products for sale. That was inflation.
Today it is different. Inflation may be the problem of the authors of the Speech from the Throne, that is the problem of a few Canadians earning $30,000 or more a year. It is certainly not the case of most Canadians.
Following the proliferation of and increase in taxes of all kinds, it is strange to hear the government make statements like the one we find in the Speech from the Throne of October 23, and I quote:
In recent months, the government has urged both the public and the private sectors to adopt special measures to combat the dangers of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy enough to forget that taxes add to the price of goods, but we must admit that the Canadian government must have a lot of nerve to inform us of its strategy which consists in uniting all possible forces, both public and private, to fight inflation more vigorously than ever.
Mr. Speaker, can we ask 75 per cent of the families in the province of Quebec whose income is lower than $4,000 per year, the businessmen who are going bankrupt, the farmers who are forced to auction live-stock, goods and implements, the industries which are folding up, the great number of people on relief, the unemployed, to wage war against inflation?
What about the 85 per cent of the Canadian population in that fight? What can they do to prevent prices from increasing?
Unfortunately, this government too often makes us believe that it does not even know why prices have gone up. I think it is time that we show some logic for, as I have already said, the Canadian problem is not one of inflation, but of plenty.
A manpower retraining program was recently launched. Small armament contracts were awarded. Subsidies were paid for winter works. Certain advantages are now given to so-called designated areas, and yet, the economic unrest is only worsening. Some ministers, some hon. members and some economists handsomely rewarded seem unaware of that, and the Canadian population is conscious of that fact and is justifiably concerned.
That is the first thing that needs to be done, and I agree with these words written by a responsible economist in the publication Ensemble on May 15, 1969:
Mr. Alfred Rouleau, president of the Co-operation Council, stated that poverty created more poverty, that the poor no longer accepted to be deprived of essentials and that the mass media tempted them to lead an easy life while they lacked bare necessities.
In Quebec, about 450,000 people (children included) receive public assistance and have a yearly income varying between $1,500 to $2,000, or $35 to $45 per week. Those are the people who live in the slums of our cities or on our unproductive farms. Add to them the low-income workers and farmers and you have one Quebecer out of five living in poverty.
At first a minimum guaranteed income should be ensured to those who are not able to work and employment should be ensured to those who can work.
In Canada, according to professor Henripin, two thirds of the poor would disappear thanks to a substantial increase in family allowances and above all thanks to the increase in the allowances according to the number and the age of the children.
Mr. Speaker, if we want to go further, an adequate policy based on our national production would allow us not to eliminate two thirds of the poor, mais to improve the lot of all the poor in our country.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
Everyone must be able to make use of the advantages of progress because our society will be soundly established only if it can ensure to each and everyone of its members not only a sufficient use of the present goods but also of all those which a truly social organization is in a position to offer them. It is only when everyone's livelihood is properly

October 28, 1969

assured that certain classes may begin to live in luxury and abundance.
The abuse of the right "to use and abuse" the advantages of social production is almost a spoliation and no words are strong enough to brand those responsible for it: the exploiters, the dishonest administrators.
Humanity has the right to live. This is the basic principle. To make it possible a proper distribution of wealth is necessary.
Goods are so plentiful in the world that the temporal needs so conducive to the practice of virtue should be honestly enjoyed by each and everyone of us. In the face of the affluence of goods produced by machines which replace him, man thus deprived of the means of earning his living has but a choice between hardship and affluence.
Pensions, allowances should result from gratuitous rights to a share of the production. Not from the outcome of the work of those who labour to earn their livelihood but only from the social capital made up of the social factors of production technology, and the machines of which we are all the joint heirs.
Mr. Speaker, in the third edition of Warning Democracy published in 1935, Major C. H. Douglas, had this to say about finance and industry:
If we consider the fact that the production of goods of all kinds per unit of mechanized worker used, and if we consider also that such energy in the last 100 years has increased by 3,000 to 4,000 per cent, three things can happen. Each and everyone of us must consume 30 to 40 times more than before and further increase his consumption as soon as the energy allows an increase in the production; or we must get rid, through exports or otherwise, of our production surpluses or else we must admit that the so-called unemployment problem is a result of the progress of applied science to industry and that we must modify thoroughly our distribution system.
Jacques Maritain wrote in his book entitled Humanisme integral, and I quote:
The law of usus communis tends to state that, at least and first for what concerns the primary needs, the material and spiritual needs of the human being, it is advisable that people get for nothing as many things as possible.
Mr. Speaker, we consider that the family represents the vital cell of society and that the real aim of the economic activities is to ensure, from the point of view of the real human good, the resources that are necessary to family life.	.
Besides, if we consider that all men have an equal right to use the earthly goods, and that with regard to the primary material
The Address-Mr. Godin needs of the human being, it is advisable that people get for nothing as many things as possible on the basis of social justice.
We consider that the fruits of production today come mainly from a social capital that has accumulated for several generations, and that the fruits of the social capital should be distributed in a social way to each and every member of society as heir of this social and cultural heritage. We hold the opinion that the guarantee of a vital minimum that would cover the primary needs in food, clothing and housing is perfectly workable today, in view of the economic conditions of production and of the production capacity in Canada.
Thanks to the advent of automation, of cybernetics and the utilization of new production techniques, we consider that the productive work of man is becoming less and less necessary and is replaced by machines in factories where automation is taking over.
Since American economists and sociologists have already stated, in an open letter addressed to President Johnson, that the first condition to avoid economic and social disorder in the present state of production which frees man from work without succeeding to reemploy him usefully is to ensure unequivocally to every individual and to every family a minimum income that would be guaranteed as a right, may I be allowed to move, seconded by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe), the following subamendment:
... that the amendment be amended by replacing the words "of large numbers of our people" by the following; "of all Canadians by the Introduction of a plan of a guaranteed minimum income."
Mr. Speaker, since the guaranteed income does not exist in Canada, the members of the Ralliement creditiste recommend that an annual income be guaranteed through the payment of a national dividend, that could represent one fifth of the gross national revenue, which amounted in 1969 to $67 billion. That would provide for security without the need to increase taxes.
I move this subamendment today because people have been talking about it for over 30 years. More recently, namely in September 1964, the Labour Gazette published the following statement from an economist, Mr. Theobald, delivered at the meeting of the 51st annual conference of the International Association of Personnel in Employment Security (IAPES) and I quote:
The effects of cybernetics revolution will be so far-reaching and so rapid that it will be impossible to provide for full employment. In other words, the efficiency of machines will keep on increasing

October 28, 1969
The Address-Mr. Godin at such a rate that employers in the public as well as in the private sectors will find It more economical to own or rent machines than to hire workers.
At the same meeting, a guest speaker, Mr. Gilles Endicott had this to say, and I quote:
Automation is compelling us to change the basic notion that there is no salary without corresponding labour. While it may seem altogether revolutionary and contrary to the Calvinist ethics on the subject, we have to accept the principle that revenue is not necessarily related to labour.
More recently, Mr. Speaker, one could read in the Thursday, September 11 issue of Le Devoir, and I quote:
The New Democrats have rushed into print in the last few days briefs that are to be used as background material for discussions at the convention which will be held in Winnipeg, at the end of October.
This week, they published, under the signature of economist Marion Bryden, another brief on the possibility of establishing a guaranteed annual income scheme.
Further on, there is an article by Pierre-C. O'Neil, from which I quote:
Marion Bryden gives an account of the conclusions arrived at by the subcommittee of the revision committee on the NDP policies with regard to a guaranteed annual income.
The committee reaches a compromise between the negative income tax, the guaranteed minimum income and what it calls a "demogrant", that is a payment made to all citizens, every month, which would vary according to the area, the age of the individual and other factors.
Mr. Speaker, here also is an excerpt from the magazine Sept-Jours dated March 29, 1969. I quote:
The Leader of the Opposition in the Commons, Mr. Robert Stanfield, also committed his party, during the last federal elections, to the concept of a guaranteed minimum income for every citizen.
But the highlight of all those discussions comes from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), and again I quote from the magazine Sept Jours:
The federal Minister of National Health and Welfare, Mr. John Munro, takes great care not to commit the government in this regard; however, he does say that, as far as he is concerned, a guaranteed minimum income is probably the normal outcome of the evolution of the Canadian social security and welfare programs.
Mr. Speaker, again I say that I moved the subamendment today thinking of the 13 million Canadians who have no income and yet have to pay all sorts of taxes levied by the governments at every level.
In closing, I trust that all the hon. members who want our country to progress will give me their support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first add my words of praise to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne for the high standard which they set for this debate and congratulate those who have spoken since for maintaining that high standard. I hope I do not deviate from it.
I wish to speak about democracy, the need for discipline in democracy, and what we, the members, may be able to do about it.
Many important issues have been raised in the Speech from the Throne and the speeches which followed. Pollution, poverty, housing, drugs, and the cost of living are without doubt important and must be debated and dealt with in a climate of urgency. But related to each specific problem and overriding them all is our guilty realization that the average citizen feels that he is voiceless, that democracy is too remote that individuals are almost meaningless. Today people are immediately informed of the issues which we discuss here, but real participation for the vast majority never comes. This will not do.
[DOT] (12.40.)
During the last decade, we have seen upheaval everywhere. Objection and protest have often descended into violence. This lawlessness has run through labour, university students and other groups. Threats and selfish force are on the increase. Just recently we had a glimpse of chaos in Montreal.
These groups which resort to violence have one thing in common-the theory that by demonstration and destructive activity their demands will be recognized. At the moment their number is relatively small, but make no mistake, they are organized and will con'inue their vicious tearing at the fabric of society until stopped. Taking their lead from tactics employed by some of the large international unions they would have what they want regardless of the cost to others or even the nation. Their lawlessness and disrespect for others, often to the extent of real cruelty, is a bayonet pointed at democracy.
The strength of the protesting groups lies not so much in their physical ability to destroy as in the atmosphere that they create-namely, that they are full of ideals and are the only ones to act on them, that it is honourable to believe that the end justifies the means and that those who do not act violently for some cause are indifferent and Slothful and therefore evil. They have taken advantage of democracy's freedom of speech
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
and freedom of protest, and by adding violence they get news coverage. They have become "the read abouts", the "listened to's" and their protests and activities have become the concern of the nation. Do the leftouts join them or some equally violent opposing group, or do they make themselves heard through direct contact with us?
The ordinary law abiding citizen is coming to believe that demonstration with violence is the only way to make his argument effective. Too many are saying it is the only way to get things done. They are beginning to feel that anything short of this results in being ignored and left out of effective participation. In some parts of the country, they think that their members are far away in Ottawa and might just as well be on the moon.
Violence and disrespect for the dignity of others has always been the birthplace of dictatorship and communism. Democracy as we know it is on the brink of extinction unless we can immediately throw up barriers of effective discipline through the marshalling of moral strength. Laws are really the accepted standard of behaviour for a community, ordinarily enforced by a minimum of personnel, but this balance is upset if organized groups, determined to put their own interests above law and society, are allowed to flourish. Once we arrive at the stage where auxiliary police and troops are required, we know that democracy is embattled.
The discipline which we must produce is not more police or troops but united opinion, of people knowing they are united, and so with sufficient power and moral authority to smother out the fires of these vandals who would destroy our society.
We cannot pretend that 264 members, no matter how hard working and willing, and we are, can alone overcome what in one decade has become a sickness in the western world, but we must attack it by every means possible. One form of machinery is immediately available, the elected representatives from each riding. We must play a greater role and become recognized as knowledgeable spokesmen for this non-belligerent majority.
We call ourselves representatives of the people but are we effectively understanding and dealing with the feelings of resentment of the vast majority who are not heard, partly because of the racket of the noisy few and partly because of our failure to transmit to them what government is doing and receive from them their attitudes toward the proposals? Even ten years ago, most people were
DEBATES	177
The Address-Mr. Chappell content to simply pay taxes and keep quiet, but today's informed public insists upon explanation and participation. Our choice is, do they do it through our leadership or by joining a protest group?
Some hon. members of the House may shy away from what is after all an enormous and pervasive problem, but just because it is so big and there are seemingly more immediate and great issues to which the leaders have addressed themselves, let us not refuse to face it. Time looks over his shoulder and questions our delay.
We must start somewhere to reproduce the sense of contact once felt between the member and his constituency. We no longer have ridings of 5,000 to 10,000 where each member knows his constituents by their first names, and the riding and its problems intimately. We now have ridings with diverse and conflicting problems, many of them international with local connotations. It is not possible to handle these as we did in the past.
The greatness of the democratic system is that we, the government, belong to the people. Increasingly in this day of paternalism and automation people resign themselves to the fact that they belong to us and in their resentment, some would cast aside the system and revert to more barbaric codes. It is up to us to reassert the basic greatness of the system by drawing more from the roots of the system and this must include being in and part of the riding at least one day a week. We have an obligation to go to the people. They have an obligation to come to us. We must hear from them. I want to hear from them and I know other hon. members do also. We recognize some protest is not only good, but necessary. However, we have been hearing the whines of a small minority, composed in part of a few half-baked post-graduate university students who are rapidly becoming professional agitators at our expense, and ridiculous demands from a few irresponsible labour organizers. They consist of a greedy, selfish, little minority. Now, let us hear the deep voice of the majority.
After a five day week in Ottawa, we have Saturdays and Sundays for our families and our ridings. A week end is not enough time to perform the service required, but to make it worse, while in Ottawa we are not nearly as effective as we could be because we do not have proper facilities.
By today's business standards our offices and facilities are archaic. If they were made as efficient as modern business or industry.
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie we could immediately become 400 per cent more effective in communicating with our ridings. It has always amazed me that democracy will spend so many millions of dollars to elect us and to keep us here, then blunt our efficiency and stifle our activity by failure to supply facilities and services commensurate with the job to be done. We do not ask these services for ourselves, but for the people we serve.
If we spent more time in our ridings we could let our constituents know that government, through their representative, is being brought to them and that they do have a voice, that they are not cut off and removed from the issues which are daily presented to them by television and press. Is it not much better that a member spend more time in his riding taking an active part in the discussion of national and local issues rather than always sitting in the House listening to what are sometimes dull and repetitive speeches, and voting like a puppet? On many occasions our votes could be registered by proxy.
[DOT] (12:50 pjn.)
Let us start with the realization that we should be in our ridings at least one day a week. It would not be our day, but their day. And better the same day for all of us, so that all of the people know that on that day government is in the ridings. If on that day we spoke to several classes of high school students and community groups we could, in a relatively short while, promote a feeling of participation and belonging, more respect for the law and government, and perhaps slow the pendulum of destructive force and, with luck, start it back.
Mr. Speaker, I hope I have sown some seeds that may grow to a new relationship between the members and the people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address you and the 
multitude of members of all parties who are poised to hear my few words, may I begin with congratulations to the mover and seconder. I listened to them with great interest. To the seconder I should say that in the Tracadie district of Hillsborough we do not grow blueberries so large that one or two would make a pie; we need a dozen or so and thereby, perhaps, enhance a variety of flavor in a blueberry pie which even the Saguenay might envy.
Thus far I have enjoyed this debate. I think there have been some very interesting speeches. But I was amazed to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) last night show his lack of appreciation for what occurred on Friday. Surely, he forgets that his own leader made the longest speech of the day. Should word get to his leader that he thought so little of all the speeches, then the angry spot might glow on Caesar's brow and the Minister of Finance might not be so comfortable thereafter.
It would, of course, be unusual if a member of the opposition stood up and said that the Speech from the Throne was the greatest, and I am not going to say that. It is platitudinous. But so have many of its predecessors been platitudinous. There are some things that I missed in the speech. For example, I waited expectantly to hear something about the Canada Development Corporation, but there was not a word. Methinks it might be necessary to appoint some kind of task force to find it again. I wonder where the former minister of finance is at the present time? Nor did I hear the suggestion that we work again at the harmonic elements of our national anthem. This, too, has been done before. The expression "the government" which was used in 1967 instead of "my government", has returned. The change from the pronoun to the article I do not understand. If it is meaningful, I should like to know what it means. If it means nothing, then why bother with these literary changes?
I notice that the Speech from the Throne tells us that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will announce items of legislation. Does this mean that the throne is being narrowed and the Prime Minister's perch being heightened? Probably it does. I remember that a Speech from the Throne indicated that we were heading for 60 days of decision. At that time frenetic activity was forecast. The founder of my party was a man of another type. They referred to him as "old tomorrow". I suggest this government is not even
October 28. 1969

"old tomorrow" or "old next year". Perhaps in the next three years we might get something done.
The "just society" has in fact become the "just wait society". Meanwhile, we shall be showered with studies, overwhelmed with white papers and deluged with reports. Never has so much study of so many issues been done with so little result. I wonder what statistician would be able to enumerate the number of reports and white papers that are already yellowing with age within the cupboards of ministers or, perhaps, on top of or under the regional desks.
If the government would like to do some studying, I would commend to them two kinds of documents for study and consequent action. These would be the many reports that the Auditor General of Canada and the public accounts committee of this house have made. If the government will follow the recommendations and suggestions contained therein, they will have a more efficient and economic government, something to which they have claimed allegiance.
Do we really need to look further into the question of poverty to be sure of its existence and its prevalence? Is it lack of information that deterred the government from taking measures to grapple with the deep-seated economic difficulties facing the Atlantic area? It is not lack of information, sir, but lack of will. Indeed, while the phrase "regional disparity" has been discovered and lip service paid to it, the government itself to this very day does, and continues to do, things which increase that disparity and make more acute the economic difficulties of the Atlantic region.
I need point only to the city of Charlottetown in the heart of my constituency where, at the present time, the government of Canada is diminishing its operations, thus creating unemployment, cutting back the effectiveness of its governmental role and contributing to a shrinkage of the economy. Can we study our problems out of existence? I fear that the promise of a remote report is no substitute for immediate action. Studied indifference is still indifference, and to this indifference the people of Canada will not pay great tribute.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
It is painful to see such a relaxed attitude in the face of so many challenges which cry out for stirring action. We live in the age of the image-makers, the hidden and perhaps
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie well-paid persuaders. Yet, we are led to believe that the image so dominates the actuality that the people of Canada will like this approach. I have actually read in the press that this is the smartest form of government, that you can consolidate anything you are going to deliver if you deliver it in three years' time. The hope that the people of Canada will go for this yellow-light document pays little respect to their intelligence or comprehension. Do we think that the people of an intelligent, enlightened country like Canada will applaud do-nothingness for three years and then when presented with-it will not be a just society; it will have to be updated-another form of panacea for the distant future will say "aye, aye, this is it". Surely, after three years of do-nothingness a great reservoir of good will will not be built up for those seeking a public mandate.
We have reached the ultimate in the ad man's technique. I read not long ago that the efficiency of the present government was marked by the fact the cabinet was now functioning under a committee system. I have never been in a cabinet, and probably never will be, but I do know that in Sir Robert Borden's memoirs he devotes a substantial portion of a chapter to writing on the division of labour in his cabinet under the committee system. To some people all that is necessary is to say such and such a thing is new to get someone to believe this is indeed the case.
While we are concerned about lack of activity, about studied indifference and about building a wall of reports between human need and governmental action, there are one or two fronts on which the government seems positively electric with activity.

My colleague says
"patronage". I am limited to 30 minutes, so cannot discuss that!
The last session ended and this one began with a zea-oing-in on the Company of Young Canadians. The throne speech referred to the "rising tide of unrest, particularly among young people". The government is now to adopt a policy long since adopted by several provinces, including the province of Prince Edward Island, to extend the voting age to 18. This is right and good. But in what they are doing they are showing contempt for the committee system and the committee of which I was a member last year. The usual procedure is that committees recommend to the House. Now, the government tells the committee
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie what to do. The vote at age 18 is good. I could not help but be very enthusiastic about this since I was early in my advocacy ol this suggestion. I wonder if it is enough. It will help. But is it an adequate response to the problems which the Speech from the Throne very rightly sets out?
I was concerned when the Company of Young Canadians was brought into the discussion at the last session. There were quotations and references to acts of subversion. I agree profoundly with the leader of the New Democratic party who asks, in effect, what has happened to due process of law and where are the courts. If there are subversives in a group, it is the courts which should be in action and the matter should now be sub judice. I am not at all happy at the suggestion, that when any official casts doubt on any governmental organization young or old, we are then immediately moved into a threepronged, two-pronged or one-pronged inquiry in respect of that organization. There may be in the Company of Young Canadians a lot of people who lack wisdom. A lot of old Canadians lack wisdom. They may make mistakes, but if they do criminal acts it is the courts which should deal with them.
What puzzles me is that here is a group of people containing only 174 volunteers, I am told, all across Canada. I may be an incredulous person, but I cannot believe that these 174 young people constitute such a threat to the 20 million people of Canada or to our political system that everything has to stop and priority has to be given to an investigation of this group. I say this because I am convinced, while there may be members of that organization who are not helpful and who are not carrying out their mandate, there are fine young people doing good jobs among the Indians and elsewhere. Does it help them to have the blanket of investigation thrown over them? The implication of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) is that if an investigation is not enough perhaps a trusteeship is what we will have. "Trusteeship" is one of the operative words of late.
Some of the Prime Minister's recent speeches have won him plaudits in the press outside Quebec. This has given him maximum exposure on the English network of the CBC.
I do not think that portion of the CBC is likely to be threatened with trusteeship. I have seen the Prime Minister on television about 11 hours over the last few weeks. It will be safe for a while. Some of the goals and values which the Prime Minister spoke
IMr. Macquarrie.]

about in his now famous Montreal speech before his own party are goals and values which are universally commended. Even those of us who are nobodies when we are 50 yards away from him cherish the unity of Canada and the preservation of the federal structure. He has no monopoly on this. Nor is he alone in realizing that, while Canadian federalism is a precious value it is also a frail fabric and requires constant support and much harmony and continued good will. We all know this.
So there is much approval for the Prime Minister's posture and his positive utterances in Montreal a week ago Sunday. It made excellent television, although as I watched the Prime Minister of Canada and the leader of the Parti Quebecois I thought that a stranger in our midst might well ask who was the moderate. But the value of the Prime Minister's performance cannot be measured by the intensity of the oratorical lightning or the volume of the forensic thunder. The final judgment will be on whether or not he has aided the forces of unity or by the vigour of his attack and the extreme nature of his suggestions has unwittingly, unknowingly and regrettably I am sure aided the cause which he sought to diminish. This is the question to which the answer has not yet come in. Might he not be enhancing the separatist cause by giving it such prominence? I wonder, I wonder.
I speak of separatism as the cause espoused by a lawful party in the province of Quebec. We have had in Canada many separatists. Joseph Howe was one. He came to Ottawa as a cabinet minister. Mr. Fielding was a separatist and came to Ottawa under Laurier. Mr. Riel was certainly a separatist and we have a stamp coming out next year commemorating him. But terrorism and separatism are not the same thing. On the question of the terrorists who would destroy our social values, the Prime Minister is right in his every utterance. As our leader said on Friday, all of us in this party are with him in his attitude and expressed firmness in respect thereto.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
I think that those who advocate separatism are wrong. Their ideas are wrong for Quebec as well as for the rest of the country, and because Quebec is a part of my country I presume the right to say that they are wrong. No portion of the country can do other than suffer economically, spiritually and in every other way if the creation of our forefathers should be destroyed and if the act of
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
faith which built a united Canada should prove not sufficiently strong for the stresses and strains of the 1960s and 1970s. But while they are wrong, they are not illegal, and the distinction between the separatists and the terrorists must be clearly made. We have had terror and we have had violence while Mr. Levesque was still a Liberal and before the Union Nationale took power and long before the Company of Young Canadians was formed.
Surely, we have sufficient faith in the political processes of democracy to meet those who would divide this country in the marketplace of ideas, and surely it is our task and duty to show the values of confederation and, something which is still more important and sometimes a bit difficult to do, to make an effort to make the values greater and more attractive. I pass no judgment, but I wonder if the slashing and the threatening is in fact the best answer. It is easy to say "we will starve out Radio-Canada and, if necessary, put it under trusteeship", and that was said; I have checked the record. These are very serious dangers. Do we have to kill the patient to root out the tumor? As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) pointed out on Friday in a most able speech-which was not adequately reported, may I say since it is fashionable now to criticize the press. A government operating the broadcasting service is the last thing this country needs in this image-making age.
There are plenty of weapons at the disposal of the government for public enlightenment or propaganda. We do not want the media turned over to the government. That is a great danger which was foreseen many years ago and which was guarded against in free states with eternal vigilance. It is regrettable that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) often seems a little too ready to slip into the excesses of threat and suggestion which of themselves are dangerous to the harmony and unity of the country, even though in the days following he tends to back off, especially if he has to face someone like the president of the CBC who stands his ground. But the explanatory notes do not always catch up with the basic text which in the first place captured the national attention. It is not for me to pass judgment upon the Prime Minister, although I am coming close to it, but I would say that after the tumult, the excitement and the hurrahs of the party faithful die down, there is time for reflection as to whether this kind of
DEBATES	181
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie sortie here, attack there and onslaught elsewhere is in fact the best kind of national leadership for this troubled country at this time.
I read an interesting editorial in the Brandon Sun entitled "Steady, There... ". It reads in part as follows:
Prime Minister Trudeau, who keeps counselling Canadians to moderation in all things, should take a bit of his own advice. The Prime Minister has thrown rather serious charges at the French language CBC, he has rebuked the French government in the strongest possible terms, and he has apparently taken rather seriously the charges that the Company of Young Canadians was involved in disturbances arising out of the Montreal police strike.
As Robert Stanfield pointed out, neither State Secretary Gerard Pelletier nor CBC President George Davidson had given any indication that an investigation of the French CBC was necessary.
Then, I go on to the final paragraph which reads:
Mr. Trudeau, like all politicians, must feel tempted occasionally to come out against sin. He did it over the weekend, blasting separatists and the French government. Maybe it's out of his system now.
I suppose there are those who suggest that the government is hoping through its actions to build up a reservoir of good will which perhaps will put its sister party in power in the province of Quebec and return it to power here three years hence.
In this connection I should like to read here an item on the Australian election. I read it not to make a comment on the Australian election, because I do not know the prime minister there, but because it is written by a very able and outstanding commentator who wrote the following after the near defeat of the government of Prime Minister Gorton. I think this is the kind of thing that our Prime Minister might want to hear, and perhaps officials of one of his regional desks might clip it out and hand it to him. It reads as follows:
... the Sydney Morning Herald said it was due to Prime Minister John G. Gorton's ''slightly arrogant, impulsive one-mand-band style of leadership".
Australia is a long, long way from Canada but I wonder if human nature is all that different, and I wonder if an intelligent electorate is so different that the same result might not be vouchsafed here.
Before I sit down I would like to say a word about the subamendment which was presented to the house a short while ago. I am

The Address-Mr. Sulatycky one of those who takes these votes very seriously. I remember some years ago when a certain great national party voted in this place for funny money because apparently they wanted to vote against us. This is not my philosophy. I am very interested in rationalizing, making more efficient and compassionate, our welfare structure. All of us should be. We are betraying our mandate if we are not
Assurances against the ravages of grinding poverty are a responsibility of the modern state, but to go on record as advocating a guaranteed minimum income in this manner might escalate, and indeed distort, the expectations of many Canadians. I believe that a thoughtful approach must include a recognition of the important place of incentives in any reformed welfare system. So, for this reason, I cannot support the subamendment. It is not often that I suggest that I carry the judgment of my colleagues on matters of policy. I do not want to burden them with that responsibility. But it is conceivable that in this case I will not be a voice crying in the wilderness or the lone voice of truth in a great and truthful party. While I cannot support the subamendment, I appreciate its presentation in this general debate and I look forward with interest to a further elucidation from the members of the party which presented it. They will probably bring forward some ideas, short of unusual currency variations, which might further inspire us all in our concern for this important matter.
So I feel that it is only right and proper, since we should all take seriously propositions, motions and amendments that are presented to this house, to indicate at this early stage that I must part company with the members of the Ralliement Creditiste who, in my judgment, are not always wrong but have a fairly good average in that field.
