speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the intentions announced in the Throne Speech is the allocation of greater funds for regional development. These are expenditures much to be welcomed. I am sure most hon. members have had an opportunity to observe for themselves the disparities which exist between various regions of the country, and even in pockets within the same region. The government is to be commended for its continuing attempts to bring equal opportunity to all citizens, no matter where they may live. Concern about regional economic disparities is not new in Canada. It has

occupied the attention of previous governments, and this government is placing increasing emphasis on the problem. Some of our developmental programs are almost a decade old. The time has arrived for an evaluation of their effectiveness. In some cases a basic reshaping of organization structure may be desirable.
I understand and accept that it will take many years to bring certain regions to an acceptable social and economic level. In many cases, the time required will be several generations. Those who expect immediate and permanent results expect the impossible. I do not suggest that we search to see if the desired ends of regional development are being attained. It may be too early to make an accurate assessment on this point. However, certain basic patterns are emerging from our various developmental programs. We can see these trends and we can project them. It is important that we make these observations and projections now to ensure that the ends of the regional development program are met in the shortest possible time.
We have had experience with various programs in the province of Alberta. Several of these are located in my riding and I shall concern myself chiefly with them. However, I should say that from discussions I have had with other hon. members, from having served on the Standing Committee on Regional Development during the last session of parliament and from my own research, my conclusions can apply to regional development programs throughout Canada.
I wish to deal first with the ARDA program. It is one of our oldest plans for regional development. It was conceived by a previous government. Large sums of money have been allocated to it and many people who should have been assisted under the program held high hopes for it. The avowed ends of the program are good. It promised an eventual end to rural poverty. In this day, when we are blinded by the magnitude of the problems of urban Canada, the first picture which becomes obscure is that of the poor farm family. ARDA promised eventual relief for such families, through programs designed to rehabilitate and re-establish certain rural people into effective employment and income opportunities.
ARDA activities in the constituency of Rocky Mountain are taking place in the area known as Census Division 14. The main current project is entitled "The Rural Development Program in Census Division 14." As with
Oclober 28, 1969

other ARDA programs, it is a joint federal-provincial program, with provincial employees providing the necessary administration.
The first ARDA activity in Census Division 14 started in 1963. Local people were encouraged to get involved. ARDA planners stated that all projects would be started only by local initiative and that eventually local residents would handle their own plans and devise their own solutions to problems. Many people became interested and did become involved. Many ideas and potential solutions to problems were offered. However, few have been implemented.
The high hopes have turned to frustrations. People no longer wish to be involved; they are disillusioned and dissatisfied. Even those persons who were originally the staunchest supporters of ARDA are now among its most vocal detractors. Today, many people in the ARDA area consider ARDA a giant hoax that has been perpetrated in order to provide employment for a few planners and sociologists. Under these circumstances, when such suspicion exists, the prospect of successful implementation of plans, regardless of their origin, is, to say the least, remote.
There are three reasons for the lack of success of ARDA, wherever such lack of success is evident. The first and most basic of these reasons is insufficient concern for people. ARDA planners often seem to be planning for the sake of planning. They do not plan in order to help people. The individual is lost in the concept of a plan.
The second reason is the failure of ARDA planners to respond to the voiced and demonstrated needs of people, of groups, of communities. The felt needs, when made known to ARDA officials, have been largely ignored.
The third cause of ARDA ineffectiveness is the rapidity with which ARDA officials seek escape from criticism under the shelter which any federal-provincial cost sharing program inevitably provides. Let me describe some of the situations which give me cause to be critical of the operation of a program which, if properly administered, would not or should not attract criticism.
The first of the disquieting cases which has been brought to my attention involves a farm couple, both of whom are nearing 60 years of age. For nine years they had lived on, and operated, a small farm. They believed that if they could clear a small additional acreage they could thereafter maintain themselves in comfort by operating a small dairy herd. An application was made to ARDA for assistance

The Address-Mr. Sulatycky with the clearing costs, but ARDA officials decided that, rather than provide funds for clearing, the small farm which the couple owned would be purchased and they would be relocated on a more suitable site. If that were impossible, then the couple were to be placed on a scheme described as early retirement.
ARDA paid $5,200 for the small farm, and after a portion of this amount was used to clear debts against the title there was appreciably less than the purchase price left in the hands of the farmer. Having now found themselves without a farm, and with only a few thousand dollars, the couple again contacted ARDA. It was then that they were told that the early retirment plan was nothing other than welfare payments. In addition, they were told that ARDA would not relocate them on another farm because they were considered too old to be starting a business. Nevertheless, the couple tried for some time to get established in other areas, but lack of resources prevented them from doing so. What I have described is certainly a case in which ARDA, rather than improving the social and economic situation of the couple involved, has contributed to a worsening of it.
In another instance, a young farmer who held a well-paying job in addition to farming a small farm was encouraged to enlarge his farm holdings. He was assured by ARDA officers that the enlarged farm would be economical and that he would be able to support his family adequately from it, and from it alone. Having received this assurance, and having been advised that ARDA would assist in procuring the additional farm land he required, he left his outside employment to devote all his efforts to establishing his farm on a better basis. Six months later ARDA officers advised him that, having reconsidered his plans, they would not now assist him in enlarging his operation as they thought it economically unfeasible. There is no reason for me to detail further the resulting implications for this farmer.
In neither of the foregoing cases was any thought given to the people involved, their needs or their feelings. There are many other such instances which I could describe. One other case deserves mention.
Some time ago the federal government committed the sum of $378,000 to assist in land clearing operations in Census Division 14. The provincial government was to match this amount. More than two years ago ARDA officials started taking applications from farmers who wished assistance to clear land.
184	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Sulatycky These farmers were encouraged to commence the clearing they desired. Many farmers applied for the assistance, paid the $25 application fee and were told to begin clearing. Hundreds of acres were opened as a result. However, when the time came to pay for the clearing no funds were forthcoming. Farmers were told by ARDA officials that minor details still had to be cleared up, and that Ottawa was blocking progress.
Every opportunity was seized to place the blame on the federal government which, in fact, had nothing to do with the problem. However, because ARDA officials could hide behind the jurisdictional shield they could avoid pressure from the affected individuals. After many months of waiting, some landclearing contractors finally took legal action against a number of farmers for the amounts owing for land clearing, and because farmers were primarily responsible to the clearing contractors many farmers had their existence threatened through seizure proceedings.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Lately Alberta ARDA officials have placed a veil of secrecy around the land clearing program and although I am told that the clearing which had been completed has now been paid for, I have not been able to find evidence of this. Perhaps I should not say that there is no evidence. The farmers who had made applications for assistance have now been approached and are being asked to pay an additional application fee of $25 because, so it is said, the $25 they paid two years ago when applications were first taken was only a deposit.
The land clearing program is to be one of the chief ARDA efforts at improving the condition of agriculture in Census Division 14. It is a program which, in fact, could help many farmers. However, many who could be helped will actually not receive any benefit because the planners who conceived of the land clearing program failed to recognize all the aspects of the scheme, and now having hardened their thoughts on it refuse, in typical bureaucratic fashion, to respond to the sound suggestions for improvement made by the people who will be affected. In order to receive assistance in land clearing, a farmer must provide a small portion of the cost himself. Although this portion is small, to the farmer whom the plan is intended to benefit, it represents in many cases all the capital resources that he can muster. The result is that, having brought more land into a useable

DEBATES	October 28, 1969
state, the farmer cannot use it because he has expended all his capital and does not have any available to invest in the livestock or machinery which may be necessary to make economic use of the new land.
Many persons have suggested that in order for the land clearing program to be fully effective it should go hand in hand with another program to assist farmers, through provision of credit or otherwise where necessary, for the purchase of livestock or machinery or whatever may be necessary, to put the newly cleared land into full productive use. It is pointed out that if new grazing land is cleared, it is of little value if the owner does not have the capital to purchase the cattle to graze on it. However, in spite of such obviously sound suggestions, ARDA officials refuse to budge from their own concepts of the plan.
The local people who still maintain hope for the success of ARDA are doing all in their power to make it work. The advisory council, composed of people from all walks of life and from throughout the ARDA area, are always looking for ways in which permanent social and economic benefits can be brought to the individual and the community through ARDA. However, of late everything is being stalled by what is being described by ARDA officials as a lack of money. Mr. Speaker, this is hard to believe when one realizes that almost $7 million has been committed in this ARDA area and very little of it has yet been spent. Furthermore, no government cut-backs in ARDA spending have been or are likely to be made. The only conclusion at which one can arrive is that bureaucratic inefficiency, tardiness and reluctance on the part of some planners to accept ideas other than their own, are being covered up by allegations that no money is being provided for the ARDA projects.
One other situation causes me concern. In our regional development programs we tend to emphasize what we have done rather than what remains to be done. We have accomplished nothing compared to what remains before us. However, even more disturbing are attempts to hold out as evidence of a successful program, accomplishments in which ARDA was but slightly instrumental. Several days ago I met an acquaintance of some years who is a successful farmer within the ARDA area. He previously farmed a relatively small holding and held other fulltime employment. About two years ago a large corporation purchased his
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
small farm for a proposed pulp mill. As a result, he obtained sufficient capital to be able to acquire a new and larger farm elsewhere. He chose an area within Census Division 14 and approached ARDA for assistance in assembling the necessary land. ARDA provided this assistance but it was hardly crucial. The individual involved could very well have made all the necessary arrangements, financial and otherwise, on his own. Now, however, this farm is a show place for ARDA. It includes a new, modern house and other necessary farm buildings. Anyone, such as visiting parliamentarians, who wishes to see what ARDA has accomplished is directed by ARDA officials to this farm.
Not very far away on another farm is a large billboard proclaiming the ARDA program in the area. It is very conspicuously placed near a large tract of newly cleared land, creating the impression that ARDA is responsible for this progress. There is no sign to rectify this false impression, pointing out that the owner's own resources provided the new land. False fronts may be necessary in the motion picture industry, but they have no part to play in the war on poverty. We must concentrate every effort on doing all that yet remains undone. Energy must not be dissipated in congratulating ourselves on our few achievements, real or imagined.
With that caution, let me now turn to an ARDA program which has proven worth while. I do so simply to support a later argument. Between Calgary and Banff is situated the reserve of the Stoney Indians. It is a magnificent setting, a broad, flat expanse of land lying at the foot of the Rockies. The Trans-Canada highway bisects it. By all measures, it is an ideal locale for a large tourist-recreational development. Some of the Indian leaders saw this possibility and with the aid of ARDA funds, a consulting firm was employed to study the feasibility and devise a plan for a major tourist development. The plan is now complete. It envisages a development which will result in a bright future for the Indian people on this reserve. The residents of the Stoney reserve look forward hopefully to the day when the plans can be implemented. It is to be hoped that ARDA will make substantial funds available for this project, just as it did for the initial study.
The point which I believe emerges in the difference between the expenditure of ARDA funds in the Stoney Indian situation and the expenditure of funds in Census Division 14 is
DEBATES	185
The Address-Mr. Sulatycky that in the former case ARDA simply provided funds but was not involved in the administration. I might note that even in Census Division 14 there are a number of ARDA programs which are producing tangible results. One of these is a retraining program. In this case ARDA is simply paying the cost of retraining individuals to enable them to obtain better employment. Again, the administrative involvement of ARDA in this program is minimal.
It is my belief, Mr. Speaker, if the money we spend on ARDA is to be put to the best use and is to result in benefits to the people whom it is intended to benefit, then the administrative participation of ARDA in these programs, both at the federal and provincial level, must be kept to a minimum. Arrangements must be worked out which will prevent the "buck passing" which now exists, and the ideas and suggestions of the people affected must be implemented by the people themselves.
There is one other phase of our regional development plan which gives me concern, Mr. Speaker. This is the type of development provided for under the Regional Development Incentive Act and which was previously provided for under the ARDA program. It is intended to increase employment opportunities in areas of the country which lack such opportunities. Generally, these are areas where unemployment is high and the average earnings are low. It is hoped that by encouraging industry to locate in these areas the income levels will gradually be raised so that eventually the disparity between such a region and its wealthier neighbours will be erased, or at least narrowed. It is now becoming clear that this is not always the case, and that in fact in many cases the establishment of industry in a designated area or region results in the solidifying or enlargement of the economic gap.
Let me explain, Mr. Speaker, how I arrive at this conclusion. When an industry, with the aid of taxpayers' money, establishes in a slow growth area the wage scales in the area are generally low. Many industries take advantage of this, as they can because of the high rate of unemployment and the scarcity of jobs, by paying wages only slightly above the local level but very much below the national average for the particular industry. Indeed, I know of cases in which the difference being paid to an employee doing the same work is in excess of one dollar per hour. That is, an
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Sulatycky employee in a plant in a designated area may be receiving $1.60 or $1.65 per hour, whereas an employee of the same firm doing the same job in a plant located in a wealthier region may be getting $2.60 or $2.80 an hour. Even productivity is not the catch in some of these cases because it can be shown that the plants within the designated areas are equally or more productive than their counterparts elsewhere.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The undeniable conclusion is that many industries have taken advantage of the incentives being provided to locate in slow growth areas and are now doing their best to maintain the lowest possible wage scales. The result is that disparities are not being corrected. In some cases a study of wage settlements show that some employees of industry in designated areas are earning less now, in terms of constant dollars, than they were three or four years ago. Wage increases in some of these plants have been, on an average, only 10 cents an hour, whereas in many cases employees in the same industry elsewhere have received over the same period increases of between 60 cents and $1.00 per hour. The result is that disparities have become greater.
We must begin to realize that industry is accepting incentives and tax concessions but is not always accepting the responsibility of maintaining and providing adequate economic situations for its employees. Often an industry which has been encouraged to come to an area by incentives is the largest employer in the area. Because of this, it has a captive labour force and thereby is able to keep wages to a minimum.
We must take a serious look at some of the situations we have seen developing. I recognize the jurisdictional difficulties in dealing with industrial matters within the provinces. However, it must be our role to point out to industries accepting incentives that they must play a role in the battle against regional disparities by adopting a positive position rather than taking advantage of the situation to increase profits while preserving an inequitable wage structure.
One further situation which I believe deserves comment is the shortage of housing in communities which have attracted industries through one or other of the incentive programs. I have within my riding one industry which was established under such a program and it has given indication that it must

close its operation because there is insufficient or inadequate housing for its employees. While I recognize that housing cannot properly come within the scope of the regional development plan, some avenue must be sought through which those communities which would benefit under the plan do not lose such benefits. At the same time, we must make certain that taxpayers do not lose the value of funds expended on the incentive program through the closing of industries as a result of lack of adequate housing.
I believe the programs of this government are right, Mr. Speaker. They are designed to strike at the problems which this country faces. However, we must always guard against the possibility that in the implementation of policies sight is lost of their purpose.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I have no wish to repeat criticisms already made about the position of the government, as revealed in the Speech from the Throne. To many westerners, the speech was notably lacking in concern for their part of Canada, empty of expressions of confidence in this country's tremendous potential and excessively pre-occupied with matters to which I, as a member of parliament and taxpayer, would not assign top priority.
It is now obvious that, having been in office for one year and a half, this administration is either incapable of recognizing today's major problem or disinterested in tacking it. I believe, together with many other Canadians, that the great problem facing our country right now is how we are to obtain the means to support our apparently insatiable appetite for so-called free services. The problem of Canadians is this: how are they to tailor their tastes to suit their purses. Over the past six or seven years, we have allowed the old emphasis on progressive national expansion and development to die away and have replaced it with a sick obsession. We are obsessed with refinements of the complete welfare state.
However desirable certain social welfare measures may be-and I am thinking of measures like the universal pension plan, hospitalization as well as medicare-they are always and inevitably exceedingly expensive. Not only is their initial cost tremendous, but they follow a historical pattern of rapid escalation in cost. The result is that a plan that was supportable when initiated in one year, becomes an intolerable financial burden through rapidly rising costs in the next year.
October 28, 1969
It seems to me that the path of wisdom and financial responsibility lies in undertaking only that which you are reasonably certain you can pay for without being driven either into bankruptcy or into the position of carrying a crippling load of debt. The average Canadian family no doubt wants a car; perhaps it wants a second car, a new colour TV set, and so on. Perhaps the wife wants a fur coat and the husband new golf clubs. The children may want assorted expensive luxuries. But I am convinced that the average Canadian family, while it may want all these things desperately, will only commit itself to buying them when it has the means at hand. Today, when some member of the family wants a special item, the wife goes out to work to acquire the means of buying it or the husband may moonlight with the same aim in mind. One way or another, through exercising personal decision and initiative, the family decides that if it wants something badly enough it must take steps to acquire more means with which to buy the desired object. My chief criticism of the Pearson government, and the government that has succeeded it, is that they bought everything in sight without taking the precaution of increasing their means. We have been guilty of self indulgence. We went for every brightly packaged scheme the federal government offered, without bothering to remember that not one of them was free and that they were all possible only through vast outlays of tax money.
There are only two or three ways of getting more tax money of which I know: you either raise rates on the existing tax base, which means that you invent new and ever more burdensome taxes, or you do what is most sensible, expand your tax base. The latter point is the one upon which Canada ought to have been concentrating. That is the meaning and purpose of national development. We Canadians must develop our economy so that it will yield more taxes without taxation becoming more burdensome. The great fault of this government lies in its having all but given up a positive policy of national development in favour of firefighting, emergency economic measures.
Canadians want and need greater and more expensive educational facilities and greatly improved health facilities. Canadians want to overcome and need to overcome poverty. These are all estimable desires and are no doubt necessary. But, and it is a big but, all these aims are very expensive of attainment and all must be paid for by public funds.
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
We see today what unnecessary friction and dispute can be caused when vastly expensive schemes grow beyond the point where it is feasible to cut them back or control them. The provinces are charged with the administration of these schemes. Their tax revenue is inadequate and they seek more from the federal government. The federal government must retain the lion's share of its tax revenues for its own particular purposes. The federal government and the provinces wrangle; they argue and exchange bitter reproaches. Even those creatures of the provinces, the municipalities, get into the act because they are at the bottom of the heap and more hard pressed for tax revenue than any level of government. Such an atmosphere makes cooperative endeavours all but impossible and as a result of such bitterness and frustration, regionalism and separatism flourish. The nation as a whole suffers. In Canada today, we must aim at putting ourselves in the position of having our cake and eating it, too. We should develop this nation to the point where it will yield sufficient tax money to carry any tax supported project the majority of Canadians may desire.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
But to do this we need leadership at the federal heart of the country. We need to be given a national purpose, with national goals and a national direction. Today, such leadership is clearly lacking. Canadians are gradually retreating into their regional shells, being suspicious of their fellows, sensitive to imagined slights and ready to magnify any grievance. This atmosphere of suspicion, distrust and inertia is the great sin of this government. It has set party advantage and personal enthusiasms above the national good. It operates on a basis of personal and political expediency. This government is guilty on many counts, but on none so clearly as on the count of neglecting Canada's agricultural industry. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, this neglect has reached a point where it has become a very real threat to a part of the national economy that cannot be allowed to die without dealing the whole national economy a devastating blow.
We in this chamber are familiar with the crisis in grain sales. The government has known about it in intimate detail for more than 18 months. The government has been strangely languid in its approach to this problem. However, it did pay sufficient attention to it to set up various task forces, study groups and councils to look into it. In faot, it

188	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Ritchie is this crisis to which the west owes the distinction of a visit from our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It is true this visit was a mixed success but it was free of the hysterical excitement that was a feature of his election campaign trail. Nevertheless he came and, if he failed to conquer, at least he saw for himself.
Unfortunately, the result of all this attention has been precisely zero. The western grain producer has been deluged with advice, laved in criticism, lectured and ignored. He is still waiting for some practical and sensible government action that will give him the hope he needs to enable him to hang on and tough it out. It is a strange attitude for a national government of a country whose agricultural community accounts for about $1 in every $8 of foreign trade and pays about $1 in every $10 of income tax.
If .the social planners who appear to dominate this government regard the agricultural community as passe and something that should be allowed to die out, surely their colleagues among the economists of government-and this government must have some of those around-can see that agriculture and the agricultural community is vital to Canada, both socially and economically. They must realize the number of industrial jobs in central Canada directly dependent upon western grain production. They must know of the railway workers, the dock workers, the brokerage firms and dozens of service businesses who depend in large part for their prosperity upon the health and progress of agriculture.
Yet all we find in the throne speech is a promise to bring in the Canada Grain Aet for amendment at some time, as though this would, by itself, in the twinkling of an eye, rectify everything. What is needed is far more than mere tinkering with the Canada Grain Act. The industry must be examined, as a whole and in all its parts.
The evolution of grain production in Canada is a story of tremendous technological and scientific development at the level of production on the farm within an old, inflexible and unchanging framework of storage, distribution and marketing. The western grain producer long ago graduated from horse-drawn equipment to modern machines but the handling, transportation and marketing line upon which his economic success depends remains in the days of the horse and buggy. Grain handling has become a question of grain storage. This is where the

DEBATES	October 28, 1969
plug is in the line and until we can devise ways of speeding up the evacuation and sale of grain, the farmer will continue to bear the brunt of slack times.
Just today the minister who answers for the Wheat Board stated that the rapeseed and flax crops would be speeded to market. This is one of the few bright spots in the grain economy at this time. As the result of a failure of the crop in Europe, the minister was able to assure the House that the delivery of the rapeseed and flax to the ocean ports would be on time.
A couple of weeks ago, according to some western newspapers, some doubts were expressed by the trade as to whether this could be accomplished. There is some evidence that some small sales of flax may have been missed by not having the grain at the port from which it would be shipped. In addition, on the west coast .there is the problem of loading ships with grain for shipment to China.
The Richardson Weekly Grain Market Letter of October 23, 1969, sets out the terms of the settlement which avoided the holding up of grain shipments to China. It states:
This will not interfere with wheat shipments to China as they provide their own boats, but exporters are having a great deal of difficulty chartering suitable ocean freight for other destinations because of the low repute in which the port of Vancouver is held by vessel owners.
Another way in which the grain industry in western Canada must be helped is to ensure that the port handling facilities can deliver on time. The elevator operators could not care less if the grain moves. They receive a steady income. The railways and the shipping interests can scramble for other business. Only the farmer is tied to the grain and when it does not move, he does not get paid.
As I mentioned previously, Mr. Speaker, this Speech from the Throne is an uninspiring document reflecting an uninspiring government. I notice that mention is again made in it to the necessity of emphasizing the government's bilingual and bicultural program. I will not thresh old straw. Everything that could be said about this program was said at the time of the debate on the official languages bill. I will simply recall my warning given at that time that this program, couched in the uncompromising terms in which it is and backed with untimely and ill-considered vigour, will do more to disunite than unite Canadians.
October 28, 1969
Already it has strained our slim reserve of good will. One need only look at the sort of thing that happened in the tiny town of Willow Bunch in Saskatchewan to realize that the picture of the relationship of ethnic groups within our multi-ethnic society is not either as simple or as easy to resolve as the Prime Minister and his colleagues would have us believe.
In closing, I should like merely to reiterate my belief that the nation's business has been set by this government on the wrong course. We should be looking outward, not continually inward. We should be pressing expansion of Canadian society and Canada's economy in every way possible, not hobbling it with regulations and inhibiting it with non-essential expenditures.
We are still young. Let us avoid being brainwashed into believeing we are prematurely old. Let us behave like a young and vigorous nation with boundless horizons before us, not like a nation that has passed its prime and seeks only to eke out an existence.

speechtext:
Thank you. I should like to consider, in the time available to me, several aspects of the affairs of the north and I intend later in my remarks to make two specific recommendations for immediate government action in this regard. First, though, I wish to take the opportunity to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau). The hon. member for Lapointe discussed blueberries in his area. One blueberry makes a pie, he tells us. I recognized there the remark of a 21362-13
The Address-Mr. St. Pierre truly honest man. He would do very well in Coast Chilcotin, because we have similar ideas. Whatever we may say, we always adhere to the truth.
I recall one man from Coast Chilcotin who visited Ontario on one occasion and spoke at great length about the height of the mountains, the growth of the timber and the expanse of the lakes in the country from which he came. After some little while his host drove him to Niagara Falls. "I suppose you have something like that in Coast Chilcotin, too?" he asked. As I say, the man from Coast Chilcotin was a very honest man. He thought for a long time before replying: "No, we don't have anything like that. But we have plumbers who can fix it." Always be honest, Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Lapointe.
Before dealing with questions affecting the Arctic I should also like to make a few general comments upon the Speech from the Throne. Last year, when I first spoke in this House, I complained about the careless spending habits of governments in recent years. I said this one had yet to prove itself. I suppose it has still to prove itself, and will be doing so for its whole term of office, however long that may be. But it does seem only fair to congratulate this government on having the political courage to trim its spending to its income.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) told the House yesterday that he expects to keep spending well below government income in the present fiscal year. This is not easily done. It is not easy for a government to trim 25,000 jobs from the civil service lists. But it needed to be done. I am one who feels that the duty of government is to govern, however unpleasant the decisions it must make may sometimes be. I sense that this government is showing the necessary courage and forethought.
I should also like to make a few observations on another aspect of government, one with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dealt during the last election campaign. He spoke of the necessity of the federal representatives retrieving some of the power of decision-making which had fallen into the hands of the bureaucracy. As a general observation in this respect I must say that the Prime Minister and his government still have a long way to go. In the long run this government and this parliament may be judged by the degree of success they achieve in taking the power to make decisions back from the mandarins. It is my personal feeling that the

October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. St. Pierre remedy may lie not in the green chamber, where debates frequently tend to be set pieces and highly partisan, but in the all-party parliamentary committees; it is these committees which may provide the instrument for operation against the overweening arrogance of some sections of the bureaucracy.
Now, let me turn to the north. The north is at this moment awakening from a long sleep and we shall not be able to order it back to sleep. Things are happening there which offer great opportunities for Canada, as well as great responsibilities and considerable danger. We cannot wish them away. We cannot say: it is too soon, we are not ready to develop the Arctic; give us 20 years to prepare for this expansion. I believe Arctic affairs entered upon a new era with the discovery of the Prudhoe Bay oilfields in Alaska. No one knows the full extent of this deposit. It amounts to at least ten billion barrels and there are probably fifty billion barrels in the reserve. Indeed, there may be 300 billion barrels, which would amount to more than all the oil ever discovered in the continental United States.
What about Canada's share? The government is involved with private industry in the Panarotic Syndicate. At the Arctic symposium held in Montreal in March of this year, one authority estimated Canadian Arctic reserves at no less than 50 to 100 billion barrels of oil and 300 to 500 trillion cubic feet of gas. To quote Mr. R. A. Hemstock of Imperial Oil Limited, the oil industry generally will then become involved in operations of the following order: the drilling of between 700 and 1,400 exploratory wells and of between 6,000 and 12,000 development wells the construction of 4,000 miles of access road, 4,000 miles of trunk road and 8,000 miles of gathering lines in addition to camps, towns, airfields and support facilities for a working population of 10,000. All this in an environment which was once considered so hostile to man that we more or less wrote it off as uninhabitable. In some of -the areas now under exploration even the ingenious Eskimo cannot survive. So far, Panarctic Development has completed two wells. It is significant that in sinking the second well they hit hydrocarbons, a gas deposit. Those who travelled to the Sabine Peninsula with the standing committee concerned with northern development two months ago are not likely to forget the sight of that gas well blazing out over the desolate tundra of the Arctic.
Here, I might digress for just a moment. It is interesting that most of this Panarctic


exploration is concentrated at Melville Island. In 1820 when Edward Parry wintered his ships at the southern end of this island he built a small handcart and led a group of sailors to the north shore. In his journal, written at the time, he noted that when the iron wheels of the cart struck the shale in some areas the shale gave off the smell of petroleum. This was in 1820. It has taken us a long time to put down the first drill.
There is another interesting feature connected with this exploration by Parry. No European visited the island again for 30 years, in fact, until the search for Sir John Franklin in the 1850's. And there, 30 years later, when McLintock visited the island, the marks of Parry's little handcart were still discernible in the soil. Here, too, there is a lesson for us: the Arctic ecology is very frail.
The United States government is showing an awareness of this fact. The permit for the construction of the pipeline from Prudhoe Bay to the southern terminus on the southern coast of Alaska must contain some of the most stringent regulations ever established in this field. I have the document here and I shall read just a few of these conditions. The company has to post a $5 million bond from which any environmental damage would be made good as far as possible. Any areas disturbed must be repaired as far as practicable. The company must file a detailed contingency plan for controlling oil spills and pipe line leaks. The government may require the realignment or modification of pipelines to meet unforeseen environmental conditions. The pipeline may have to be re-routed around areas with unstable soil conditions. Great care must be taken to avoid melting the permafrost. Passages for fish must be provided in all cases where a pipeline crosses a stream; it must be buried underground, not laid on the stream bed. Construction may be halted to protect key wildlife areas during seasonal nesting activities and fish migration.
o (3:20 p.m.)
There is more, but clearly the United States government is showing an awareness of the dangers of development in the north and Alaska. This is one of the dimensions of the problem which we Canadians will have to consider, and consider very soon. It could affect our own territory very shortly, particularly if, in addition to the Alaskan pipeline, we see a pipeline coming down the Mackenzie to bring Prudhoe Bay oil, and hopefully Canadian oil, to the markets in the centre of the continent.
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
There are other methods of moving oil which are under consideration. There might be a pipeline across barren land to the port of Churchill on Hudson Bay. Canada's Herschel Island might become a sea port for Prudhoe Bay crude. But what has caught our attention most of all during the past year has been the Manhattan project.
I am not going to go into the details because I think hon. members are quite familiar with them. An amount of $39 million has been spent by a consortium of oil companies, headed by Humble Oil, to see whether a specially strengthened United States supertanker could smash its way through the barrier of ice that lies in the Northwest Passage. A subcommittee of our own Standing Committee on Northern Development went north in August to meet the Manhattan and to welcome the initiative taken. As the record shows, we pointedly welcomed them to Canadian waters, with the accent on "Canadian" waters.
At the moment the Manhattan voyage appears to have been a partial success only. The hope and expectation was that this heavily strengthened ship could smash the ice barrier in McClure Strait. The plans of Humble Oil were gigantic in scope. If this experiment were successful, then by the second quarter of next year, 1970, the company expected to let contracts for 250,000 ton supertankers. Their long range goal was to have two of these tankers a week pass through the Northwest Passage, 52 weeks a year.
To what extent their enthusiasm has been moderated by the experience in the north, I cannot say. However, we must note that the Manhattan did not succeed in forcing her way through the polar pack ice in the McClure Strait. In fact, she behaved pretty much in the manner that our own coast guard people predicted; she became beset, and the John A. Macdonald, a Canadian icebreaker, had to free the vessel. She then sailed south through the Prince of Wales channel and, to the surprise of nobody,, got through in that way to the opposite side of the archipelago. But it has been an exploit and will add very considerably to scientific knowledge of ice conditions. Again, we should congratulate the spirit of enterprise of those concerned, and we look forward to the time when this valuable information about ice will become available to us.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, since Canada's attention, as so often, has focussed on the deeds of people of other nations, I do not
DEBATES	191
The Address-Mr. St. Pierre suppose that many Canadians noticed that it was a Canadian ship the Chesley A. Crosbie, which this year scored another notable first in the north by sailing to within 500 miles of the geographic north pole. This is the farthest that any commercial vessel has penetrated north of the North American continent.
The shipment of dry cargo is one matter. Quite another is the shipment of oil. It is this continuing Manhattan project-it is continuing as far as we know-which also poses, in addition to the great opportunity provided if the project is successful, a major danger to the Canadian Arctic. Many ships have been lost in the Arctic, invariably in the same manner. They become beset by the ice. They are nipped by the ice and, when released by the movement of the ice away from the sides of the ship, they sink.
To lose a tanker containing a quarter of a million tons of pollutant in the form of crude oil in the Arctic would be a disaster greater than any man-made disaster of this kind the world has ever seen. But what I wish particularly to draw to the attention of both the members of the government and members in all parts of the house is that we really do not know how bad the situation would be since there has been a complete lack of research into the subject.
The waters of the passage range in temperature from 27 to 31 degrees Fahrenheit. A little closer to the continental shelf the temperature is between 33 and 35 degrees. However, we do not know what will be the action of crude oil spilled into water of this temperature.
It is suggested that oil spilling out into water of this temperature would probably form a gelatinous mass. When it reached the shoreline, where it might be exposed to temperatures of 50 below, it might turn into a hard plastic. The only information that I have been able to find as to its behaviour is that this pollution might last for decades, and possibly for centuries. Most crudes contain poisons, some of which are as lethal as DDT.
I did say, Mr. Speaker, that I had two subjects to which I in.ended to draw the government's attention and urge immediate action, and this is one of them. I suggest that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources should immediately institute a full program of research in Arctic waters using Prudhoe Bay crude oil to provide us with a body of fact. Since we are the nation most immediately concerned in this matter, ours is the government which should initiate such studies.
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. St. Pierre This is not a question that we should turn over to other nations or leave to the investigation of private companies. The government should ascertain as early as possible precisely what is the result when crude oil, and especially Arctic crude oil, is spilt in sub-freezing temperatures.
My second point is associated with the first one, and I will make it now. What is the potential of our Arctic fisheries resource? We have known for years that there are a great many species of mammals and fish in the Arctic waters. Many Eskimos have formed co-operatives and are canning some of these sea foods for sale in the south. But how great is this particular resource? Is it over exploited or, as is more probable, under exploited? Might there not be room for considerable expansion of this industry?
I questioned the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) about this in the fisheries committee last year, and his answer was to the effect that, as far as he knew, Canada had never surveyed the fisheries resources of the Arctic. We simply do not know how extensive are these resources in Canada's third ocean. I suggest to the minister that now is the time to make this discovery, and to do so not simply for the immediate benefit that an extension of Eskimo fishing operations would bring. It may be that in this regard Canada will become engaged in debate in the United Nations or elsewhere. Our people will want to speak of the value of our marine resources in the Arctic, and our case will scarcely be strengthened if we have to admit publicly that we really do not know what they are. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, these two departments of government can and should be undertaking this valuable service with all possible speed.
These are just a couple of aspects of Canada's great duty to protect this area of our country, and this, of course, inseparably involves sovereignty. The waters within the archipelago are Canadian waters, and we must make this clear to the world community.
I suggest there are two things we must make clear. First, we must make clear that we welcome commercial shipping in these waters, as we have always welcomed such shipping in Canadian waters. It would be intolerable if it were suggested that this country close the passage to the shipping of the world, assuming that such passage were made possible by modern day technology.


[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
But simultaneously we must point out that this nation will decide what constitutes innocent passage and that we will close the passage to vessels likely to cause intolerable damage to the waters or land of Canada. Perhaps in the United Nations we shall see developed a new regime for oil shipments on the world's oceans. I hope so. It is needed. The Prime Minister has indicated that his government will press for this and I think we should welcome the Prime Minister's statement. However, the possibility of such a development does not relieve the government of its clear responsibility to give its prime attention to Canada's sovereign seas. The prime duty of this or any other government is to act first in what it conceives to be Canada's national interest. Of course, we must have among us who will say, nay. I note in an edition of a Toronto paper for December 16 that the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) is reported as suggesting Canada should declare these waters to be hers. He is quoted as saying:
Our legal experts tell us we wouldn't have a chance before the International Court at The Hague.
When he refers to "our legal experts" I wonder whether he is speaking perhaps of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson who, on October 21 at a NATO meeting in Washington, said:
Permanent ice should be assimiliated with permanent land. The government would be well advised to do the utmost to ensure that Canada has control in the Arctic, especially since it is possible that nuclear weapons will be deployed there.
Or perhaps he was speaking of Dean George Curtis who, on behalf of the Canadian government, made extensive investigations in respect of our land sovereignty in the early fifties at the time the DEW line was being started. When speaking before the Canadian Bar Association in Ottawa he said that Canada had a very strong case for drawing base lines around the tips of these islands and declaring them to be Canadian waters. I could go on to deal with the remarks of Dean Cohen and others who have spoken on this subject. There is no certainty in these matters. There is never any certainty in matters of international law or in any legal matter. I am satisfied, however, that our position is very, very strong.
There is not time for me to review the many theories on international law, but they are numerous. There is the hinterland theory
October 28, 1969
from the Greenland case. There is the Norwegian system which permits the drawing of base lines around the Arctic archipelago. There are the rights of exploration, discovery and continuous and effective occupation. Neither is	the	case of Indonesia comparable with our Arctic archipelago, although we are told the United States leans toward that view. Indonesia is an ocean archipelago. In our case, the Arctic is an extension of the continental land mass. International shipping has moved for a thousand years through the Indonesian islands. International shipping has never moved through the Canadian Arctic without the Canadian government's knowledge and, frequently, with Canadian government assistance as indeed was the case when the John A. Macdonald accompanied the Manhattan.
It is suggested that the United States government would hail us before the international court. They would seem to be in a rather poor position to do so because the United States subscribes to The Hague court with a proviso, the Connolly amendment. I am sure if they chose to take this stand it would not take this parliament long to pass its own reservation, its own Connolly amendment. It is suggested that the United States government might favour using another nation to serve as its running dog in this situation. But what nation? Norway? Hardly, in view of the fact that it has a base line system. What nation then-Japan, Peru? Perhaps. I am convinced it is not only in the Canadian national interest particularly but in the interest of the United States government and all governments that Canada should control these waters. The best and only sure control is to make it clear to the world that they are ours.
The Prime Minister has spoken of a threepronged action-legislation to establish conservation regulations in northern Canada, a statement on Canadian sovereignty and, finally, the inducement of the United Nations to act. Like many members on both sides of this House I eagerly await the details, but since in the last session I was critical of what I considered to be government inaction or even indifference I now wish to express a feeling of gratification at the considerable progress shown to date. I think it is also most gratifying that members of this House, and Canadians generally, are showing keen interest in our vast northern territories.
In closing, I should like to quote from the journals of Warburton Pike, a sportsman who spent much time on the barren lands at the
The Address-Mr. La Salle turn of the century. One of the quotations is this:
A dweller In cities Is too wrapped up in the works of man to have much respect left for the works of God, and to him the loneliness of forest and mountain, lake and river, must ever appear but a weary desolation.
Probably this feeling pervades in much of Canada although, as I say, there have been some encouraging signs of genuine interest by Canadians in the vast northern reaches of our land. The second quotation I believe in some sense might answer those who say that the Arctic is far away; it is cold, inhospitable and really what value can it have. I suppose the answer is that beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Pike had an Indian guide named Saltatha who was approached by a missionary priest. This is Saltatha's answer to the priest:
My father, you have spoken well; you have told me that Heaven Is very beautiful; tell me now one thing more. Is it more beautiful than the country of the musk-ox in summer, where sometimes the mist blows over the lakes, and sometimes the water is blue, and the loons cry very often? That is beautiful; and if Heaven is still more beautiful, my heart will be glad, and I shall be content to rest there till I am very old.
I thank hon. members for their courteous attention, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all warmly congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau), with whom I am better acquainted.
While listening last night to the laudatory comments on their speeches, I understood that there certainly will be a most valuable pool of candidates at the next convention for the leadership of the liberal party. There is no doubt in my mind about that.
I would also take this opportunity to congratulate my leader for his excellent speech a few days ago. I have read carefully the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and I am under the clear impression that it is full of good intentions.
Of course we would have preferred to find in it very concrete and valuable information. We get the answer that details will be given in the white papers which will be presented

October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. La Salle during the session. So we shall continue to hope for a few months.
At the beginning of my remarks I would like to take the opportunity to congratulate the Prime Minister for his recent decision to appoint an ambassador to the Vatican. Indeed I have long realized the justification for such a move.
I have heard or read the speeches of other members whom I would like to congratulate for having expressed their views and presented to the house the needs of their constituents. Some parts of the Speech from the Throne deal more particularly with my area or constituency and I wish to make a few comments about them.
Firstly, I would have liked, as so many others in Canada, to see my constituency included in the designated area program. I thought I had made sufficient representations to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion who was co-operative and provided me with a very interesting file. Indeed, following thorough studies and information given me about my constituency, I had thought that would be enough to warrant the designation of my constituency.
Of course some arguments were put forward to me, such as the economic consequences of the vicinity of the city of Montreal. Indeed, that city is 40 miles away. Those consequences were valid while Expo was on, but today, they are not. As for the international airport which could be beneficial to my constituency, I am quite sure that we will only feel the advantages of that project, in three, four or five years.
Until such difficult years are upon us, I would have liked the reasons for our representations to be considered as valid. I still hope that, through further representations, the government and the minister will agree to come back on their decision and to grant to my region this advantage that other regions already possess.
There is something also about housing. The matter was discussed throughout the last session. I am convinced that the measures referred to in this house last year will not be sufficient to give the building industry the push it needs.
Last year, it was suggested to facilitate loans and to set easier terms for repayment. I think that, as long as this loathed 11 per cent sales tax on building material is maintained, the problem is not seriously faced.
This tax is very heavy today for those who want to build a house of their own. Moreover,
[Mr. La Sailed
as long as no serious thought is given to granting loans for housing at a rate of 5 to 6 per cent to workers who earn $10,000 or less a year, the government can dream up a number of measures, publish fine White papers in which it offers ever more attractive loan and repayment facilities that may extend over a period of 40 years, without however giving to those who earn from $5,000 to $10,000 a year the opportunity to own their own house.
I am also wondering if the government is taking these considerations seriously, since I raised the matter last year. Furthermore, other hon. members spoke about it last night and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) referred to it.
Therefore, I do not see how on a short term basis it is possible to get the construction industry going again. We should think more of the pride that the worker takes in owning his own house. He very often becomes quite another man in the community. To own one's home is at the same time being able to take part in the social activities of his parish or of his riding. That could help the worker to become more useful to society.
I think the government should examine the possibility of granting loans for housing at 5 or 6 per cent interest and, if necessary, of making up the difference between those interest rates and the prevailing rates. Since the building industry affects a large percentage of Canadian workers, a higher employment rate would bring more taxes to the government.
Last year, I had hoped, when we debated a non confidence motion on unemployment, that the people drawing unemployment insurance benefits would become more productive.
Though regretfully I must recognize that this system is now spoiling a generation. It is unthinkable to continue to increase unemployment insurance benefits and to leave those people unemployed when municipalities are in a precarious financial situation with insufficient funds. It seems to me that the government should intervene and that such a proposal could be studied by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). Municipalities could avail themselves of the services of those men who would get a weekly pay without having to spend a cent.
Very often municipalities-in my region as elsewhere-have work to be done. Their main concern is always the same: the budget.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I wonder if it would not be a commendable and profitable gesture for our country to
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. La Salle
allow our municipalities to put those men to work at no cost at all. Those who would be inclined to refuse work would not deserve to be paid and we know very well that most of those who collect unemployment insurance benefits and welfare allowances are able-bodied and willing to work.
In so doing, we would help our municipalities carry out some projects. In fact, there are in my area several rivers which are an eyesore because their banks are poorly maintained. We could fix them up, perhaps not as well as those of the Rideau canal, so that tourists might be tempted to visit our municipalities a little more often. That would also represent an extra asset for the municipality.
I think this is a suggestion that should be taken into consideration by the government, in order to make a high percentage of our workers more active than they are now, because if the government claims that it is better to pay them for doing nothing, I still think most members would nevertheless wish that such action be taken. I dare hope they will support me in this.
The throne speech also dealt with reforms in the welfare system. I imagine that there are many things to be done. We are told that the forthcoming white paper will bring us the answer. I think every member of my party, including myself would like nothing better than to discuss this matter thoroughly and to undertake sweeping changes.
I must not forget to mention the importance in my constituency of the tobacco industry.
Tobacco growing is a feature of my constituency where are to be found 90 per cent of the cigarette tobacco producers in the province. Many things have been said on the subject of tobacco. The producers in my region are really worried and rightly so. I was informed after the sale of tobacco last Friday that so far prices have declined from 20 to 30 a pound, due to the fact that companies feel uneasy following the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) last year.
The Committee has met several times and some people have acknowledged the danger created by smoking while others have tried to prove the opposite. One thing is certain, we know a lot of people who never smoked as well as smokers who died of cancer. Of course 80 per cent of the people who die of cancer are smokers, as 95 per cent of the Canadian people smoke.
However, the leaders of the Tobacco Growers Association assure me that they are definitely prepared to negotiate, to discuss and even to help the government, in every instance where an improvement could be made. In my opinion, the goodwill shown by the tobacco producers deserves a special consideration from the government.
What has particularly surprised me is the attitude of the government as a whole in this regard. During a trip which I made in New Brunswick with the committee on agriculture, the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Levesque, assured us that he could count on further appropriations to improve the soil for tobacco growing and to extend the lands. I congratulate him on his efforts to promote that interesting industry, which moreover does nothing but benefit the Department of National Revenue.
However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare goes to great lengths to frighten people by telling them that tobacco may produce cancer, and I fail to understand the attitude of the government because it is prepared to allocate additional funds to improve tobacco farming while at the same time advising people to quit smoking.
I wonder what is the opinion of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) about this, especially when earnings of the tobacco industry are reported close to $500 million. Of course, it is a noble gesture for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to stand up for public health. I would agree with him if an attack could be launched against abuses that may lead to cancer.
Tobacco is not necessarily the only form of abuse. It is the case also of alcoholic beverages and so on. It is surprising to note that people singled out one industry which after all represents several millions of dollars. Everyone knows that the Tobacco Producers' Association is prepared to negotiate with the government and to co-operate with it in every way.
Therefore, I urge the government to show a more responsible attitude. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) must agree to continue the promotion of the product, if justified, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare must come to an agreement with the Minister of Agriculture; finally, the Minister of National Revenue must tell us what the Canadian tobacco industry is worth in terms of dollars.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that an important industry in my riding will no longer be
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. La Salle harassed. If, unfortunately, tomorrow morning tobacco should no longer be in use in Canada, I would want the government to find a solution for all the producers in my area and for those in Ontario who are in greater number.
I hope that the government will accept to deal with this question a little more seriously than it did last year. Co-operation must exist between the Departments of Agriculture, National Revenue and National Health and Welfare.
I will take the liberty to give my opinion after spending one year in the house. As many other hon. members, I probably had to listen to some lengthy and sterile debates in order to bring about changes in our procedure, some of which were excellent. We even limited some debates which had not made me sick anyway.
Goodwill should also accompany those reforms and those measures. As an individual, before coming to parliament, I heard all sorts of observations. The people often seemed to have lost confidence in their elected, because of protracted debates and representative flippant speeches.
In addition, some members reneged on some of their commitments. It is always easy to make promises on platforms, but once in the house it is at times difficult to work objectively. Sometimes, it is difficult for some members to support good legislative measures.
I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that in the coming session, the Canadian parliament will regain the confidence of the electorate. I should like parliament to be more practical and especially more objective. I hope that we will all work together in this house as administrators and not as politicians.
What I said publicly I shall repeat here in this house: We must work with objectivity and uphold the truth more often. We will need a lot of courage. I cannot accept that we should limit ourselves to politics in this house. I feel that there is room for politics during election campaigns. So much the worse for those who overdo it, so much the worse for those who deal especially in the political outbidding.
I dare hope and believe that some day we will see, in Canadian parliament, a courageous and serious opposition that can support the good measures which the government introduces. I also hope that the government will respect and accept the suggestions of the

opposition that could improve the proposed legislation.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
If in all fairness, we took that stand, we would make good the promises that we made during the electoral campaign. It is perhaps the great fault of parliament of lacking objectivity at the right moment. Therefore, I venture to think that it will be possible to show such objectivity not only in the interest of the members but also of society.
I wonder if one can go as far as to say that the interest of society must come before that of the party. Personally, I would be inclined to think so and I am ready to devote my time to safeguard, first, the interest of society through a political party which grants me the right to speak in order to defend the aspirations of my constituents.
When I speak about objectivity I do not mean that we must abstain from saying what must be said in this house.
In this speech from the throne, many problems are mentioned. There is one perhaps that was not brought up, through lack of courage or fear of causing disunity in the country. The problem facing Canada is that of Quebec. Perhaps it would be easier not to mention it in order to avoid more or less laudatory remarks, but this would also show a lack of frankness and of courage. There is between Quebec and Ottawa a link which could not be defined during the last session, even with the great promise of a just society.
What is a just society? This concept may be difficult to define, but I think that attempts are made every day to find its true meaning.
The problem of Quebec is surely quite as important as any other. Indeed, it is a constitutional problem which was hardly mentioned in the speech from the throne. We wonder if the time has not come to concern ourselves with the status of Quebec within confederation. We should put to work to the committee appointed to set up the basis of a new constitution. I believe the time has come to settle the matter with objectivity and to discuss it in all good faith here in this house, as well as with our colleagues from the other provinces. People should no longer be led to believe that here, in Quebec, there is only a minority eager to have a new constitution which will define, once and for all, the place of Quebec and its aspirations, as well as the guarantees of its fulfilment within the Canadian nation.
October 28, 1969

No one dares acknowledge that Quebec is in a particular situation. At least, no one seems to be willing to raise the subject in the house lest it should hurt the feelings of certain members. Some venture to say that there is in Quebec a group of independentists or "pequists".
It has often been alleged, in press conferences, for instance, in order to reassure the rest of the country, that they were nothing but a few people of no importance at all. 1 truly believe that what they call in Quebec the third provincial party is something quite serious. This is likely to be a matter of wonder for some, of concern for others.
We have three parties in Quebec and that hostility which might have been due to the question of the new constitution has been with us for the past ten years. One may reproach Quebec-and the federal government through its prime minister, for whom I have much respect, often did so-for not knowing where it is going as far as the constitution is concerned.
The Quebec government, through all its premiers has quite often stated its position on the constitutional question since 1960.
Quite recently, working papers on the constitutional question were made public. Moreover, the Quebec government had the opportunity of expressing its views very clearly on educational radio, pollution, mining rights, international relations and medicare.
Then, why would a storm burst so often on the question which has been asked on numerous occasions during the years 1960-62: what does Quebec want?
Attacking some personalities in the Quebec government, ministers or public servants, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did a few days ago in Montreal, on the pretence that these ministers or public servants are alone responsible for all the federal-provincial problems, is, I think, a major mistake. Such a mistake is all the more serious as it was committed by the Prime Minister of Canada himself, a man whom I would have expected to be better informed and less prejudiced.
We must not forget that the re-exoneration of the present federal system is not done by a few people only but rather by a major section of the population, and this remains a continuing concern for Quebecers, no matter who is in power in Quebec city.
The constitution has been challenged for several years now and it is pure stubbornness to refuse to face the facts and to think that
The Address-Mr. La Salle only a few people in Quebec want a reform in depth of the constitution.
Of course many observers think that the present government won the elections in the rest of the country by implying that it was necessary "to put Quebec in its place".
The only question I ask the government is: "What really is Quebec's place within Confederation?"
A few days ago dangerous words perhaps were said in Montreal in a flight of oratory. Quebec as it is today has been described in somber and tragic colours and everybody has been condemned indiscriminately. The attack on the legally constituted authorities in Quebec and in the City of Montreal has worried more people than it has reassured.
Much publicity was given to those who want to divide Canada while, in the same breath, it was being said that those people represented a very small minority of the population. If such is the case, why does the Prime Minister give so much attention to the matter? On the other hand, if this group is really large, one has the right to ask whose fault it is.
Quebec as it is today definitely refuses to accept the interpretation that is being given to the Canadian constitution. That may be annoying to the government and it has proclaimed throughout English Canada that it would control Quebec and would put it in its place. I suggest that the matter must be discussed in this house, in the most objective manner possible, because Quebec refuses to yield in spite of those comments.
Under such circumstances, I understand the impatience of the federal government as well as that of the provincial government and the citizens of that province.
Allow me to say a few words about the Quebec-France agreements.
The Canadian government is acting today as if it were sorry to have agreed in 1965 to the establishment of direct relations between Quebec and France. Did it perhaps feel then that those France-Quebec agreements would be of no consequence?
We realize today that those agreements have become quite important, precisely because they meet the needs of Quebecers.
The government of Canada is worried about that. It would like to take over the whole matter, while the agreement concluded with France in 1965 aimed precisely at easier and more direct relations between Quebec and France.
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. La Salle
The government ol Quebec has been accused of picking quarrels over protocol. I wonder how to characterize the attitude of the present government which would like any French minister or official who intends to visit Quebec to go and bow in Ottawa, even when it is not necessary.
I am very anxious to get explanations about this. Could there be one law for one's friends and another for one's foes? I would like to know.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, before closing, I should like to ask again for the drafting of a new constitution in which would be enshrined the guarantees needed if the citizens of Quebec are to prosper. I therefore demand that a special debate be held on this subject during this session and that a free vote be taken then.
I rely, of course, on the support of Quebec members to give a clear and faithful explanation of the particular situation prevailing in the province of Quebec and of Quebec's special needs. Being assured of their good faith-

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues for having granted me two more minutes. This is all the time I need to round up my speech.
I therefore request that we hold a special debate in this house, Mr. Speaker, not only for the benefit of Quebec but also for the benefit of the whole of Canada. I feel that we should have the courage and sincerity to discuss quite openly with our colleagues from the other provinces the importance of this constitution in the interest of Canada and of Quebec. To refuse this debate which would be bound to enlighten the minds of Quebecers as well as of Canadians, would be to agree with those who already imagine that Quebec's sovereignty would be a solution to the problems of that province. I hope that those remarks will be of a kind to produce positive and favourable results.
I said that I was relying on the support of the hon. members from the province of Quebec who understand better than anyone here in this House the importance of defining, once and for all, the role of the province of Quebec in Canada.


In my opinion, it would be beneficial to the province of Quebec to remain part of Canada.
I am one of those who believe that Canada will also benefit by it. The province of Quebec will then remain one of the fair provinces of this country. However, one would need courage and objectivity to study that question' and to define it precisely, for the matter of a new constitution has been discussed for ten years. We are growing impatient, and the present situation, for those who dream of the independence of the province of Quebec, is perhaps the result of that too long awaited reply which never comes from the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, I have made those remarks, imbued with great objectivity-at least that is my opinion-in the belief that I was serving not only my province, but also my country.
