armed forces will be cut from about 98,000 to between 80,000 and 85,000 men and that some bases around the country will be closed. The defence spending cuts will keep defence expenditures within a $1.8 billion ceiling, which represents about 17 per cent of our total expenditures.
Spokesmen for organized labour stated last week that wage restraints would not be acceptable. It is natural that they would be very reluctant to agree to wage restraints until they see some evidence first of a moderation in prices, rents, interest rates and other costs.
It does appear from what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said in the House last night that the monetary and fiscal policies of the government are beginning to have the desired effect of reducing inflation. However, the inflation psychology is still in evidence and it is certainly to be hoped that a broad form of voluntary restraint of wage and price expectations in all segments of the public will come about. There is no question that wage controls-and you could not have one without the other-are inherently very distasteful and extremely difficult to enforce. However, if the ever increasing cost of living is not soon checked, I believe our federal government will have to consider seriously commencing consultations with the provinces-which have the constitutional jurisdiction over price and wage controls, except in wartime-to decide on the best way of implementing such controls.
With respect to high taxes, the public has a difficult time differentiating between the taxes levied by the different levels of government. In metropolitan Toronto, our municipal taxes for municipal and school purposes are a heavy burden on the homeowner of modest means. Here, our Provincial Liberal party is advocating that 80 per cent of education taxes should be paid from general provincial revenues. Such a policy would reduce school taxes in Scarborough by about two thirds. The 5 per cent provincial sales tax affects people on modest incomes much more than it affects those with higher incomes. On the federal level, the freezing of expenditures in most government departments, as well as the reduction in the public service and the armed forces above mentioned, will reduce the amount of income and other taxes that would otherwise be needed. However, it is expected the white paper on tax reform, to be released on November 7, will contain many proposals which will make our federal tax laws more
21362-14J
The Address-Mr. Weatherhead fair and equitable. We are all waiting eagerly for this report.
The Speech from the Throne also mentioned the issuing of a government white paper on social security in the next few months. In this regard, the future of family allowances has been speculated upon. In my second report to my constituents last June one of the queries in the attached questionnaire concerned family allowances. A great number of constituents replied, and 30 per cent were in favour of cutting off family allowances to those families earning more than $7,500; 30 per cent wanted to leave the allowances as they are now; 20 per cent wanted to abolish them completely and 20 per cent wanted them increased or had other comments. Since some $600 million is spent annually on this program, it is natural and wise that it be reviewed. However, as a father of five small children, I know how my wife looks forward to her monthly family allowance cheque; and from the heavy correspondence on the subject that I received from the riding I firmly believe that most of the moneys now being paid as family allowances are being spent wisely by the mothers concerned for food, clothing and school supplies for their children. At this time I would, therefore, be very reluctant to see any substantial change in family allowances unless new government policies adequately compensate families of modest means in particular.
We have heard much in recent months about various guaranteed income schemes, and I certainly hope that the white paper on social security will make particular recommendations with regard to this. I must confess that a year or two ago it seemed to me that a guaranteed income plan would only be possible at some distant date. However, I now believe that Canada cannot afford to wait long for such a plan. It is absolutely essential that we should provide a sufficiently high minimum to give every Canadian the opportunity of a decent standard of living, along with the maximum incentives to encourage recipients to seek work and training.
A year old experiment in New Jersey with negative income tax using 400 families appears to have been successful and is an improvement over their current welfare system. The experiment will continue for three years and eventually involve 1,000 families. Under that plan, a family of four is receiving $3,000 from the government if it earns no income at all; $2,500 from the government if it earns $1,000, for a total income of $3,500;.
200	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Weatherhead $2,000 from the government if it earns $2,000, for a total income of $4,000 etc., until the point is reached where it will receive no additional moneys from the government at all if it makes $6,000 a year or more.
The recent plan of President Nixon is somewhat more modest. It gives a maximum payment of $1,600 to a family, with aid ceasing after the family's total earnings reach $3,920 a year. As a result of the New Jersey experiment, it is estimated that the cost of a similar plan for Canada will run at between $1.5 billion and $2 billion above our current welfare programs. This is certainly a great deal of money; it is about the total cost of our annual defence spending. A more modest plan would cost less and a considerable amount of money could come from greatly reduced federal government spending on family allowances and Canada assistance plans, which now total about $1 billion.
Accordingly, I believe that as soon as our fight against inflation is won, which one way or another should be fairly soon, we should immediately proceed with a guaranteed income plan that combines maximum incentives to work with obtaining retraining, an adequate income base being guaranteed by the government. At the same time, the proposals of the white paper on social security will give us the opportunity to re-arrange and rationalize our many diverse and overlapping welfare programs. Many of these programs could be eliminated or partly replaced by a new guaranteed income scheme. However, there still would be some Canadians, because of physical or mental handicaps, that would require additional welfare over any guaranteed income base, and so it is not realistic at all to state that a guaranteed income plan would replace all of our current welfare programs.
[DOT] (4:20 p.ra.)
A guaranteed income plan, no matter how good, will not in itself eradicate poverty. The hundreds of millions of dollars the federal government gives to the provinces toward post-secondary education, its student loan policy which give the opportunities of higher education to almost all who can benefit from same, combined with the excellent occupational retraining and manpower mobility programs of the Department of Manpower and Immigration, are additional requirements. The new incentive programs of our Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the underdeveloped areas of our country are also very

DEBATES	October	28, 1969
necessary. However, these various federal policies, combined with a guaranteed income plan, would go a long way toward the discontinuance of the poverty cycle in these underdeveloped areas and among the disadvantaged groups of peoples, including the urban poor in Canada, where it now exists.
The plan indicated by the federal government to transform its unemployment insurance system into a more broadly based income maintenance program, and to add nearly one million Canadians to those eligible for benefits, would supplement and possibly supplant some of the guaranteed income plan ideas. Out of a labour force of 8.1 million, some 6 million are now covered by unemployment insurance and the proposed new coverage would increase the coverage to 7 million. Some 200,000 to 600,000 receive benefits every month.
At present, only workers earning up to $7,800 are covered and are required to pay weekly contributions. Under the new plan, it is understood that the ceiling will be raised to include employees receiving much higher incomes, perhaps all salaried persons no matter how high their pay. As the Toronto Daily Star said in their lead editorial yesterday: This means in effect a new tax on the well-to-do tor the benefit of the poor. Contributions from higher income specialists and executives who are rarely out of work or in need of help will swell the unemployment insurance fund for the benefit of lower paid workers for whom unemployment is a real threat.
The added revenue obtained in this way would make it possible to increase the now too low benefits paid to those who are out of work and would also make it possible to extend the maximum period for which benefits can be received beyond the present period of 52 weeks. The apparently proposed addition of sickness and maternity leave benefits would also be most welcome.
While a general guaranteed income plan will have to wait until the fight against inflation has been won, I can see no reason why the old age security and guaranteed income supplement to our senior citizens cannot at least be increased annually at the same rate as the cost of living. I do not think I am being inconsistent in advocating this while agreeing with anti-inflationary measures in general. The Throne Speech reiterated the necessity of increased government spending in regional development programs and those dealing with our Indians and Eskimos. I believe increased pensions to our senior citizens are of equal urgency.
October 28, 1969
Certainly, we should not overlook the fact that by bringing down the qualifying age over the last five years from 70 to 65 as of January 1, 1970, our government has benefited a great number of our senior citizens. Of course, the Canada Pension Plan is greatly benefiting more and more of those people reaching 65. The old age security pension of $79.58 as of next January 1 is received by some 1,600,000 Canadians and some 780,000 of them receive additional moneys through the guaranteed income supplement which in January will give our senior citizens a maximum of $111.41 a month. However, at present, the old age security and the guaranteed income supplement can only be increased 2 per cent a year, while the increase in the cost of living recently has been considerably greater. Accordingly, I believe that as a minimum the necessary legislation should be amended to allow an annual increase in these pensions of at least the same percentage as the annual increase in the cost of living.
A general guaranteed annual income plan discussed earlier would particularly benefit our senior citizens and this is one of the reasons I believe it should not be long delayed. However, if the dangers of inflation prevent it from being initiated soon, I would think that the present amounts of the old age security and guaranteed income supplements paid to our senior citizens should be reconsidered. An increase in our old age security pension of $10 across the board to the 1,600,000 receiving same would mean $190 million more that would have to be paid from the federal treasury.
While this might have some advantages politically, it would be giving considerable money, in total, to those of our senior citizens who are fairly well off, and who would not really need it. Such an across the board increase of, say, $10 would also make little appreciable difference to those who depend entirely on the old age security and guaranteed income supplement. Accordingly, I believe that along with automatic, annual increases in both the old age security and guaranteed income supplement to completely cover annual increases in the cost of living, the government should increase the maximum of the guaranteed income supplement by $25 a month.
Such an increase in the guaranteed income supplement would cost the federal treasury between $120 million and $150 million a year, but it would be received by approximately a half million senior citizens who are in most
The Address-Mr. Weatherhead need, those who have really no other income. However, it was these people 65 years and over and those approaching that age who did so much to build and develop our great land, who made sacrifices in the two wars, went through the depression and had so much to do with our post-1945 economic expansion. I firmly believe that we have an obligation to more adequately take care of them.
I believe also that the federal government, in its capacity as an employer, has a special obligation to increase the pensions of its retired civil servants, particularly those who have been retired for a number of years and who are trying to keep body and soul together on pitifully small pensions. These people directly worked for the good of our country over long and difficult years. Our government would not only be giving them well-deserved help by increasing their pensions, but would be leading the way, by example, in persuading the provincial and municipal governments as well as private businesses to do the same for their retired employees.
During the summer recess I had the privilege, as a member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, of taking part for three weeks in the hearings on the government's white paper on the report of the Woods Commission on the Canadian Pension Commission. There are about 950,000 veterans in Canada, of whom about 166,000, including widows, receive disability benefits under the Canadian Pension Act. Of the 148 recommendations of the Woods Commission, the government in its white paper accepted all but 30 in whole or in part. A new and more independent appeal division, the granting of basic 50 per cent minimum pensions to all Hong Kong veterans who have any disability at all, additional payments to the multiple disabled, a broader "benefit of doubt" clause with respect to evidence of disability presented by veterans, are some of the proposals contained in this white paper.
While we have held 23 meetings and heard 57 witnesses from the Department of Veterans Affairs, the commission and all the major national veterans' associations, we intend to hear considerable more evidence before preparing a report or reports. I have been very impressed with the high calibre of these witnesses and their devotion to the needs of their former comrades. I am sure I can speak for every member of our committee when I say that our minds are still open and we will carefully consider all the evidence and representations before preparing our final reports.

October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Weatherhead [DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
There are very important items in the Speech from the Throne which I shall not have time to discuss in any detail this afternoon. Perhaps a few can be mentioned, however. Water pollution is a subject of increasing concern across the country and though much of the constitutional responsibility for its control lies with the provinces, the proposed Canada water act which would designate as a water quality management area any body of water in which there is a significant national interest and provide fines of up to $5,000 for every offence, will help co-ordinate the fight against water pollution in this country.
In the course of my speech during the budget debate last June I discussed in considerable detail the need for the federal government to continue to take an active interest in policies designed to promote new housing in our large urban areas. I personally praised the many amendments to the National Housing Act which we passed last spring. These, together with the amendments to the regulations, should help considerably in this regard. I was happy to read in the Speech from the Throne of the government's commitment to seeing that one million new housing units are built in the course of the next five years and that particular attention is to be paid to satisfying the housing needs of low income families. Latest figures show that we are presently ahead of last year's pace in housing starts and there is every indication that these will total more than the required 200,000 for 1969 by the end of the year.
The discovery of an enormous oil field near Prudhoe Bay in Alaska and, more particularly, the voyage of the United States Manhattan through the islands of the Canadian Arctic have brought home to us the tremendous potential of our Arctic resources. Some concern has been expressed as to whether we have been exercising our sovereignty over these territories. However, both the Speech from the Throne and the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during this debate last Friday show clearly that there is absolutely no question as to our sovereign rights, not only over the islands of the Arctic archipelago but over the continental shelf which lies under the water between them. The Prime Minister also made it clear that the government is determined to take every step necessary to protect the natural environment of the Arctic waters from pollution by foreign ships.

Nor have I had the time in which to discuss new consumer protection legislation dealing with packaging and labelling standards, the identification of fibre-content in textiles and compulsory safety requirements for autos, including exhaust controls. Similarly, the subject of imminent new legislation having to do with wire-tapping, bail and the Expropriation Act reforms might have been discussed in some detail-and these are only a few of the many important matters dealt with in the Speech from the Throne.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the government on proposing the reduction of the voting age to 18 years. I had the privilege last year of being invited to many of the schools in my riding to discuss issues with the students, and of playing host to many classes from our schools when they visited Ottawa to see parliament in action. I found the students well-informed, inquisitive and intelligent, with a real concern about the problems and injustices in the world. Decreasing the voting age to 18 will mean that some 1,200,000 more young people will be entitled to vote. Classes in civics, political science and related subjects in high school will now become more meaningful and from the age of 18 our young people will, from now on, exert a significant influence on Canadian governments and policies. I am certain this influence will be very beneficial to our federal parliament and to the country as a whole.

I wish to join those who have offered congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address. They did a good job with the meagre material with which they had to work. It must have been difficult to arouse much enthusiasm for some of the platitudes which are larded throughout the speech. The lead editorial in the Ottawa Journal of Friday, October 24, expresses this very well under the heading: "A smug speech Trudeau gave Michener". I quote:
Poor Mr. Michener will not have felt very comfortable uttering some of the yawn-like statements on the state of the nation which Mr. Trudeau put in his hands to read from the Throne.
''Notwithstanding the fears of people of little faith it was encouraging to find in Canadians in all ten provinces and in the Arctic islands that their sense of identity and of the potential which Canada offers to them and to their children is strong and healthy."
So all who are disturbed about disunity and disparity and disruption of purpose are merely "people of little faith?" They might gain more faith if this government and all gpvemments and
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
politicians showed more concern and determination to deal with the clouds we all see over this country.
Who are these people of little faith? Would they be the unemployed, those who cannot find work even in the affluent society we hear so much about? Would they be those who cannot find decent housing, those who have been waiting so long for this government to provide a housing program not just for the rich but for those who cannot afford down payments and who cannot pay high mortgage rates? Or would they be the civil servants who are being made the scapegoats for this government's so-called war on inflation? The President of the Canadian Labour Congress, in a recent statement in Ottawa, dealt with this aspect very well. I quote from this statement:
The federal government's action in firing civil servants is one of the most brutal and callous decisions ever taken by a government. These civil servants and their families are being needlessly sacrificed to satisfy a government policy of austerity, a policy which at best is highly questionable at this time.
We already have a high unemployment rate in Canada and this latest move by the government will only serve to aggravate our unemployment problem. If the government felt that it was really necessary to reduce the size of the public service, it could have adopted other means of accomplishing this without resorting to outright dismissals. It could, for example, have depended entirely on the normal attrition process of not filling positions as they become vacant. Instead it has chosen a policy which can only lead to the demoralization of the entire public service. The long established principle of security of tenure has been destroyed. The government, instead of displaying exemplary conduct as one of the biggest employers in Canada, has selected a course of action which can only tarnish its image in the eyes of prospective employees who will think twice before joining the public service.
This is not a situation which is peculiar to Ottawa or to one region of the country. I find when talking with civil servants in my area that there is a general disillusionment with the service. There is a real breakdown in morale because no one knows when the next cuts will come, no one knows whose job will be declared redundant. Where is the encouragement or the inducement to join the civil service as a career? In my own city of Moncton, as is the case all over the Atlantic area, lay-offs have been announced in government departments and many loyal workers with as long as 25 years service, including veterans of the second world war, have felt the weight of the government's axe.
I would be the first to agree that inefficiency and waste should be eliminated from the
DEBATES	203
The Address-Mr. C. Thomas civil service. But this process should be carried out selectively, not with the axe but, rather, by judicious use of the pruning knife. Cut out the fat, but don't destroy the lean in the process. Does it not constitute a confusion of purposes for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), on one hand, to recognize that the Atlantic area is one of regional disparity where special measures must be taken to create new jobs, while, on the other hand, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) contributes to unemployment by throwing people out of work?
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Where are these people going to find other jobs, Mr. Speaker? Do you fight inflation simply by throwing people out of work? How do you explain to these people that they must make sacrifices when the government itself is making no effort to cut back? How can you explain this move to such people when they know that there has been no cutback in the staff of the office of the Prime Minister? His office costs have jumped to $350,000, compared with $150,000 when his predecessor was in office. His advisers now number 117, at a cost of $1.5 million. It is pretty hard to go to a civil servant who has suddenly been laid off, who has received no compensation other than one week's pay for each year of service, and explain to him why he has been laid off when he knows at the same time that the government has made no effort at all to cut back its own staff.
The editorial in the Ottawa Journal on Friday, October 24, to which I referred previously, continues in this way:
The Government has come belatedly and Inefficiently to the fight against inflation. It was only in August Trudeau announced it was now time to "cut the fat" from Government operations, though Louis Rasminsky and most every other authority in the land had been urging economy for a dozen years. A few days after announcing the fat would now be cut, the Government stated it would spend $600,000 to renovate Ottawa's old station to make nice party rooms for Government conferences-a building that is to be torn down in five or six years anyway.
To tell the Governor General to imply to the country on behalf of the Queen that the Government has done its duty against inflation and now it is up to the public-is to tell Canadians they are fools.
When the cabinet originally announced its decision to eliminate some 25,000 jobs from the federal civil service, it assured us that this would be done without too much dislocation of employees since most of them would be eliminated through the normal process of
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. C. Thomas attrition, resignation and so on. I, personally was assured by senior officials of various departments that every effort would be made to place redundant employees in other jobs that would become available through retirement. This procedure was understandable and acceptable, but within a few weeks the Prime Minister announced that he was ordering a freeze on hiring in the civil service. Even though there were vacancies in certain departments, these vacancies would not be filled.
This is in direct contradiction to the original policy statement of the government and can lead only to hardship and the destruction of morale in the public service. We now have the anomalous situation in the federal civil service where certain departments that are short staffed have openings, where there are qualified people laid off in other departments-clerk 4's, accountant 3's, whatever they may be-who can fill those jobs, but because of the Prime Minister's directive these people cannot be placed.
On October 17 the gravity of the situation in the Atlantic area became so evident that it prompted me to send the following telegram to the Prime Minister and to the President of the Treasury Board:
Announced layoffs in Moncton office of supply and services plus rumored layoffs in other government departments and agencies in the Atlantic area are causing great anxiety in the civil service and are a direct contradiction of stated policy that this is an area of regional disparity entitled to special consideration. This action will increase the disparity between Atlantic region and the rest of Canada and is compounded by recently announced freeze on civil service hiring which makes mockery of assurances that these people will be absorbed by other departments. I therefore urge that you honour previous commitments by immediately suspending freeze on hiring in Atlantic area until all affected persons are either absorbed by other federal departments or until the Department of Regional Economic Expansion initiates long awaited policies to provide them with other employment. The gravity of the situation transcends sectional and political considerations and demands that we present a united front. I am sending a copy of this telegram to all Atlantic M.P.'s requesting that they meet in Ottawa within the next two weeks and present the Atlantic case to your government.
Copies of this telegram went out to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson) and to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), but I regret to say that up to the present day the only acknowledgement has been from the secretary to the Prime Minister. This is another indication to me of the complete disregard that this government has for the problems of

the Atlantic region. Although they pay lip service to them time after time, when we ask for action we are completely ignored.
I might say that many of my own colleagues replied to invitation indicated their appreciation of the problem and promised their support. I am now appealing to all Atlantic M.P.'s to present a united front to see whether we can get the action our area deserves.
The Speech from the Throne contains this paragraph, as reported at page 2 of Hansard for October 23:
History, geography and economics have placed certain of our citizens at a disadvantage.
We in the Atlantic area do not need to be told that.
Under legislation enacted during the last session of Parliament, the Government is establishing programmes to reduce these inequalities.
I think all members will agree with that and will say "Amen". But we have heard that said so often over the years. We are always given promises for the future. The Atlantic area has been studied and restudied. There have been white papers, commissions,, surveys of all types, to the point where we must now be the most analysed people in the world. White papers and studies are fine, Mr. Speaker, but unless they are followed up with proper, comprehensive action, they are nothing but a waste of money.
All members of the house from the Atlantic region welcomed the formation of the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion. While it was not everything we desired, we did feel that at long last here was a department that would co-ordinate all of the various programs in that area, with the object of formulating a competely new concept of regional development which would bring our area up to some sort of parity with the rest of Canada.
I welcomed the report tabled in the house yesterday by the minister, his first report. While there is not a great deal in the report, I want to congratulate him on assisting in the establishment of the first new industry to be set up in this area. However, we need a great deal more action than this if we are to reduce the disparity that exists between the Atlantic area and the rest of Canada.
I also agree with the concept of growth centres. I think this is a much better approach than the old scattergun approach of granting assistance whenever it was requested. However, before growth areas can attract
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
new industry they must have the infrastructure-a word I do not like but which seems to be a common term nowadays-to encourage industry to settle. I prefer to call this requirement social capital or social overhead. In other words, in order to attract new industry to a growth centre you must provide the roads, the transportation facilities, the land banks for housing the workers who will come into the area, sewage facilities and those municipal services that the municipality concerned probably cannot afford to finance on its own.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
This is the area in which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion should be doing more than it has been. It is all right to attract industry or attempt to attract it. However, the first thing industry will ascertain is whether the area has housing for its workers, whether it has proper transportation facilities so it can ship out of the area and whether there are proper facilities for pollution control and so on. I urge the minister and the officials of his department to speed up action on these problems. I know several municipalities are ready with development plans but, as always, are hampered by lack of funds. One of the most pressing problems in the city of Moncton is the nine level railroad crossings in the city proper. Over the years it has been recognized there must be a complete relocation of tracks in the area to free land for industrial purposes and to eliminate most of the transportation problems. The city has gone ahead on its own and, indeed, in the last week has developed an excellent study through the co-operation of consultants. I appeal to the minister and the officials of his department to give this proposal serious consideration when it is presented to them.
The people of the maritimes for months and years have been hammering at the fact that they must have a completely new and comprehensive transportation policy for the region. We were all quite encouraged in June when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) made the statement in the House, in presenting his new bill, that he would collaborate with the premiers of the provinces in the appointment of a committee to discuss this whole problem and come up with a comprehensive policy on transportation. I, for one, was greatly disturbed, as I believe were all members of the Commons transportation committee, when the minister's statement that he was again suspending the freeze on freight rates appeared in the press. I suggest to the
DEBATES	205
The Address-Mr. C. Thomas minister that this was a breach of faith with the people in the Atlantic area. They were given verbal assurance in this House that changes would not be made in the existing structure until such time as the new committee came up with an over-all program. This has caused a great deal of concern in the area. I should like to read from a recent editorial which appeared in the Saint John Telegraph Journal:
Just within the last week it was learned that the railways proposed to cancel less-than-carload freight service into the region November 3, leaving only the substantially higher express rates for small shipments. Then the Federal Transport Minister said he had asked the railways to defer the action.
But he promptly threw another uncertainty into the situation by announcing that a federal-provincial committee was studying the idea of eliminating general transportation subsidies within the Maritime Freight Rates Act territory-a 20 per cent federal subsidy on the cost of moving goods from point to point within the Atlantic Provinces and eastern Quebec-in favour of using the funds in a concentrated way to assist a limited number of commodity groups or selected geographical areas within the region. That leaves everyone wondering whose costs go up 20 per cent and whose go down.
We need a new transportation policy, without a doubt. The rest of Canada got a new deal in March, 1967, and this region was promised one at that time.
But we also need a reasonably stable situation now and until that new deal is worked out. The present bewilderment harms existing business and hampers development.
I confirm this editorial statement. Shippers in the region are now at a complete loss to know what rates to expect on certain commodities. They do not expect lower rates; they know they will go up. There is complete confusion there now because the shippers do not know what transportation costs will be involved, in connection with the merchandise they have to move. This to me would seem to be another typical example of the way this government has operated over the past year. With all their talk of participatory democracy, consultation with the people, the fact that they will sound out all shades of opinion to get theses and antitheses and arrive at syntheses *-all good phrases-they will show a complete disregard for the wishes of the people and certainly show a complete lack of co-operation with the provincial authorities. Lubor J. Zink, in the Toronto Telegram for October 22, 1969 under the heading "PM shows contempt for democracy" said:
It is the product of the contradiction in Mr. Trudeau's theory and practice of government.
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. C. Thomas
In theory, he postulates "participatory democracy", i.e., direct and presumably constant involvement of the electorate in the process of Government ...
In practice, however Mr. Trudeau negates what he preaches.
His method of Government shows contempt for any form of democracy; it is secretive and authoritarian.
Far from going to the streets, he does not even go to Parliament with his decision-making process.
A very good example of the way this government completely ignores parliament is the recent action of the Minister of Transport in appointing his Atlantic transportation committee without notifying the House or consulting it. He at least might have had the courtesy to tell us who the appointees were and who the members of the committee were. The press report stated that the committee had met in Halifax and had taken certain action. I think, however, that the Minister of Transport at least should have had the courtesy to let us know what was being done. The article continues:
His policies are hatched behind closed doors by anonymous task forces, in secret conclaves with hand picked technocrats, and they are announced as Prime-Ministerial edicts.
Where Parliamentary approval is still necessary, even after Mr. Trudeau's emasculation of representative democracy, his decisions are presented to the Commons by a docile Cabinet as Government policy, and rammed through by the docile Grit majority.
To expedite the rubber-stamping process, and make it foolproof, Mr. Trudeau wound up his institutional retooling period by putting the muzzle of Rule 75C on the Commons last July.
How accurate a description that is of the method by which this cabinet operates! There are many examples of this complete disregard for parliament and the committee system. The mover of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne made a statement that cooperation among the parties is necessary to get things done. I say to him I am glad there is one member on the government side who recognizes there must be co-operation by the opposition parties if there is to be hope of getting legislation through. But to get co-operation one must deserve it, one must earn it.
How can the government earn co-operation from this side of the House if it ignores completely the niceties of parliament, ignores the work of the committees, and if decisions are taken by the cabinet while the committee is still discussing policies. There are many examples of this. This type of thing happened so often in connection with the work of the

transportation committee that now the members of that committee know their work does not mean anything. It happened in respect of the agricultural committee and the committee on external affairs. Co-operation cannot be obtained unless it is earned. In closing I should like to quote again from the Ottawa Journal of October 22, 15 months after the election. This editorial was written before the Speech from the Throne was delivered, when great things were expected. We have heard so often that this was to be the session of action in which so much new legislation would be introduced. This was to be the Trudeau year. Mr. Pearson was left behind. The Journal, together with other papers, naturally expected great things. This is what it wrote:
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Fifteen months after the election, the glowing Liberal campaign speeches of 1968 are overdue promises to pay on which the government must make good or face the disappointment and scorn of the electorate.
This government is obviously again postponing action which should be taken and they are doing nothing to relieve the hard-core problems of unemployment, under-employment, inflation, lack of housing and pollution. Therefore, I most heartily support the amendment put forth by my leader.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the time-honoured custom of extending congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, I wish to join those who preceded me in congratulating the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) for their exceptionally interesting contributions which dealt in part with the history and natural aspirations of their respective constituents. I also wish to take this opportunity to extend my personal congratulations to the two new Ministers without Portfolio and to the two new parliamentary secretaries. In these appointments the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has recognized ability, hard work and dedication.
The Throne Speech reflects the sincere desire of the government to give the people of Canada the best government possible in the times in which we live. The Ottawa Citizen of Friday, October 24, 1969, summed up the real intent of government concern on subjects of primary importance to every Canadian such as peace, poverty, youth, individual rights, consumer rights, pollution, grain marketing, the underdeveloped world, inflation, tax
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
reforms, housing, etc. It is a program aimed at achieving economic and social goals, a program which has never been found in any previous Throne Speech since I have been a member of this House.
In the matter of peace, I doubt whether there is a country in the western world that is more concerned with peace than Canada, and it has been the traditional concern of Liberal governments to promote international friendships as an ideal for peace. The evidence for everyone to see was our action in sending a peace force to the Gaza Strip during the Suez crisis in 1955, action which won for Mr. Pearson the Nobel Peace Prize when he was Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs, and more recently in sending the Canadian peace force to Cyprus. The action we took at that time was generally considered to have averted a possible war.
In the matter of poverty, the war on poverty is not an empty phrase but is a serious attempt which shows that the government means business. This is evidenced in its policies which are designed to achieve a just objective. Perhaps it is not irrelevant to point out that a Senate committee under the chairmanship of my good friend Senator Croll is about to hold across the country hearings on the question of poverty in the various regions of Canada, with the end result being arriving at recommendations to be made to the government on how best to deal with this internal problem which all of us, regardless of party, would like to see solved. I should like to remind hon. members that it was Senator Croll who first suggested the supplementary income benefit of $30 per month to pensioners, who need only fill out a simple income tax form in order to qualify; and this additional benefit is now pegged to the cost of living.
Speaking about poverty, the question of a guaranteed income for all Canadians will have to be examined and studied. The concept of an all-embracing welfare plan which would guarantee a minimum income is a very attractive package if and when we can afford it. Personally, I am not against it; nor is any member of the government. I believe the idea should not be shelved in a remote pigeonhole, but rather should be studied by a competent committee of economists who are removed from political influence. Such a committee could serve the government well in an advisory capacity.
On the subject of youth, I believe that the proposal to amend the Canada Elections Act
DEBATES	207
The Address-Mr. Badanai to lower the age of voters to 18, as mentioned in the Throne Speech, is welcomed. Various reasons can be advanced for lowering the voting age. First of all, I think it is the logical development of a process which has been going on for a long time, especially since the last world war when youths of 18 were entrusted with technical and often dangerous assignments. As everyone knows, originally the right to vote was greatly restricted by one means or another and for many years it was considered the privilege of a few. The age of 21 was presumably selected because it was considered an age at which a person reached maturity; but because conditions have changed greatly over the years, the Prime Minister has wisely decided in this matter, as in other fields, that the time has come to break new ground and lower the voting age to 18. This move is in line with his intention to channel the enthusiasm and energy of our young people into the mainstream of Canadian political life, instead of letting them loose to agitate authority and take part in irresponsible and often subversive activities.
When speaking of youth one cannot ignore the criticisms leveled at some of the activities of the Company of Young Canadians. I have personally received several communications from my constituents complaining about certain activities of the members of the Company located in Thunder Bay. The concept of the Company of Young Canadians and its objectives are worth preserving, notwithstanding the adverse publicity with regard to the activities of a few unqualified people who are probably unfit to serve in this noble experiment.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The Company should not be disbanded, but I would certainly dismiss anyone with subversive motives whenever those motives are brought to light. I believe it is a sound decision of the minister to have the activities of the Company investigated by a parliamentary committee. The minister has promised a thorough investigation and whatever action may be necessary to attract capable and qualified young men and women to make their just contribution to the betterment of Canada.
The inflationary trend of consumer prices in recent years has affected not only Canadians but the people of every country in the western world. Long ago the government took steps to meet the problem, which is not one of easy and immediate solution. As soon as the
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Badanai Prime Minister took office, sensing the concern of the nation about the spiralling cost of living he lost no time in appointing a fulltime minister in charge of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. With characteristic zeal and drive the new minister began his difficult task of controlling unscrupulous credit and advertising practices. I am confident that his dynamic and serious dedication will bring beneficial results. I am sure that the protective legislation envisaged in the Throne Speech will be translated into measures beneficial to all concerned. In the meantime, I should like to mention that anyone wishing to offer a suggestion about goods and services should write to Consumer, Box 99, Ottawa. This is part of the service furnished by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Now I wish to say a word about pollution. The Speech from the Throne stated:
Through the United Nations and its agencies Canada is seeking to establish a system to combat pollution of international waters which threatens so many forms of life on this planet.
With public concern over pollution growing steadily, more and more thought is being devoted to the organization of pollution control and to the roles that the various governments must play, because it is not just a federal responsibility; it is also a provincial and municipal responsibility. It is also an international problem. The late John F. Kennedy had the problem of pollution in mind when he said:
The race between education and erosion, between wisdom and waste, has not run its course ... Each generation must deal anew with the raiders, with the scramble to use public resources for private profit and with the tendency to prefer short-run profits to long-run necessities. The nation's battle to preserve the common estate is far from won... The crisis may be quiet but it is urgent.
For several years an International Joint Commission has been studying pollution in the Great Lakes and as a result it is expected that some action will be forthcoming in the near future. Recently statements have been made blaming the pulp and paper industry for polluting our waters. It is my understanding that the industry has been concerned with the problem; indeed, some companies have spent considerable sums of money on efforts to control water pollution. The Great Lakes Paper Company of Fort William has taken a lead in the installation of controls in the district of Thunder Bay and it is to be hoped that its experiments will soon bear fruit. The

Logger, a publication dealing with the woods industry, recently reported:
The Ontario Paper Company Limited will spend $5,000,000 on a three-stage pollution abatement program over the next two years, Company President Robert M. Schmon announced.
However, I would hesitate to advocate measures so strict that they would force plants to close down. I think that in this matter, as with other problems, patience and discretion must provide the guiding line to the achievement of an eventually satisfactory solution. The Department of National Health and Welfare has conducted an extensive program on the evaluation and control of air pollution, the result of which will in all probability be the enactment of a national clean air act. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in a policy statement on pollution at its last annual meeting, made the following recommendations:
1.	That the federal government co-operate fully with the provinces and the United States in investigating existing pollution control legislation and in developing truly effective measures for environmental pollution control.
2.	That since tax incentives are allowed industry regarding expenses incurred to prevent water pollution, suitable incentives relating to air and/or land pollution be accorded industry.
I fully endorse the Chamber's proposal as one of the best means of meeting the problem of pollution. In recent months a great deal has been said about a capital gains tax. The Carter Commission on Taxation, whose recommendations after nearly three years still have to have practical effect, did a great deal to create endless discussion on the pros and cons of a capital gains tax. Canada is a growing: country, it needs a constant supply of development capital. The Carter Report recommended a capital gains tax. It specifically mentioned its value as a deterrent to land speculators who in recent years have made huge profits on the demand for building sites. In that area a capital gains tax would be justified. However, other factors must be considered before we can apply such a tax equitably. The tax structure would have to be devised in a way that would not prevent a shortage of development capital. Perhaps a limited capital gains tax could be devised which would meet present day conditions.
The arguments of NDP members against, the effects of American investment in Canada are typical of that party's attitude toward the United States, an attitude which is consistently hostile regardless of the benefits to-Canada which American capital has brought
October 28, 19G9

by creating jobs for Canadians. Mr. Earl McLaughlin, Chairman and President of the Royal Bank of Canada, is reported to have said in a speech recently that the reason we have so much American investment is that investors have faith in a prosperous, growing Canadian economy. He emphasized that Canada's future prosperity and growth depend on a continuing inflow of investment capital from abroad.
Does foreign investment mean foreign control? Mr. McLaughlin does not believe so. Investment by Americans, Englishmen, Frenchmen, Italians or Germans is not made by their governments; these people are not arms of their respective governments, and Canadian companies owned or controlled by foreign investors are good corporate citizens and must conform to Canadian laws. The business behaviour problem of foreign investment is a false problem and the fear of foreign domination from this source is a groundless one; it is as irrational or neurotic as the fear of foreign debt
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, press reports to the effect that the reserve forces of Canada will be reorganized consistent with the announced proposed changes in national defence policy, and that such reorganization will see a strength reduction of 50 per cent in the militia nationally, with the possibility of larger reductions in Ontario, have sparked a sizeable body of public opinion against such a move. I have received several letters and a brief from members of the Senate and honorary appointees of Thunder Bay militia units, the Lake Superior Scottish Regiment and the Lakehead Service Battalion, urging the maintenance of our militia without curtailment.
It has been pointed out that the militia units suffered under a series of post-war reorganizations and curtailments, culminating in the major changes of 1965 which reduced six units to two in Thunder Bay and restricted them in the Port Arthur armoury. Few other than local residents realize that in essence geographical and transportation reasons confined the militia to the city of Port Arthur as far as the area of Thunder Bay was concerned. With the formal amalgamation of the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur taking place on January 1, 1970, the units will be in a much better position to service the whole community and additional enrolment may be expected.
The Address-Mr. Badanai
From the standpoint of economy, I understand that the savings involved in the reduction would be insignificant. What is more important is that the 400 or more young people who have enrolled in the militia at the Lakehead have added materially to our safety and protection which the very presence of the uniformed force affords in case of need. The militia also provides a valuable place for many young men to profit by their experience; it is helping them to develop healthy citizenship. I express the hope that before any action is taken to curtail this valuable means of citizen protection in cases of emergency, the matter will be re-examined.
Having taken an active interest in immigration ever since my election to the House of Commons, I should like to reiterate what I have been saying for years, namely, that every effort should be made to ensure a continuing flow of immigrants to Canada as a consistent policy. The flow of immigrants in 1966, 1967 and 1968 reached a respectable number. This year, however, the flow appears to be tapering off at an alarming rate. As a matter of fact, it began to drop in 1968.
Some time ago a Toronto industrialist, himself an immigrant, called for the large-scale immigration of unskilled workers in the fields of mining and agriculture. He said that both fields were starved of workers, which meant lower productivity and higher cost. Yet the very area in which this successful businessman observed the greatest need had the sharpest drop in .the 1968, and worse, still, 1969 immigration figures.
I know that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) is very much concerned with the need for filling up our empty spaces by following an aggressive policy of immigration that is consistent with our economy. Speaking in Vancouver a few months ago he stated that since 1950 more than 27,000 business ventures had been started in Canada by immigrants. They have involved almost $355 million in working capital-and these are only the new immigrantheaded firms that are known to the government. There are probably a great many more. Those 27,000 new businesses have provided employment directly for 82,300 workers since 1950, many of whom are also immigrants. Indirectly, of course, the new ventures have created many more jobs. The immigration figure for 1967 was 222,876. In 1968 it fell to 183,974, a drop of 38,902. For the first quarter of this year the figures show a 14 per cent
October 28. 1969

The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
drop in comparison with the same period in 1968.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to your attention a question which for years has been the concern of not only my constituency but the entire region of northwestern Ontario. I refer to the discriminatory freight rates which have had an adverse effect on established industries and are a deterrent to prospective industries. The problem of transportation has not just to be viewed from the point of view of benefit to southern Ontario. Freight rates to northern and northwestern Ontario are unrealistic, and I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) to give consideration to having this matter referred to the Parliamentary Committee on Transport and Communications for a thorough review of every aspect on the situation.
On September 27 last, during a visit of the Prime Minister to the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur-which was part of a successful tour of northern and northwestern Ontario-the mayor of the new city of Thunder Bay asked that the announcement of the advent of the new city which will come into existence on January 1, 1970, be made in parliament. Such an announcement would stimulate and inspire the more than 100,000 citizens to strive to make their new city one of the best in the country. The mayor also suggested that the new city, rich in Indian history and lore, should be considered a suitable area for the establishment of a research centre on Indian affairs. I am very happy to endorse both proposals and I hope that the Prime Minister, whose visit to my constituency was one of the highlights in the community, generating enthusiasm and affection, will give favourable consideration to both suggestions.
Mr. Speaker, the Throne Speech has revealed a carefully planned program designed to give Canadians legislation to fit the times. The Prime Minister is to be commended for his determination to listen not only to his professional advisers but for seeking the views of the people in the streets of the nation. This, I believe, has helped translate the suggestions made to him informally by both young and old into the policies outlined in the Speech from the Throne.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my turn, I wish to congratulate the mover of the Address in reply to the

Speech from the Throne. He took that opportunity to make a very objective review of the economic and social situation in our country and of the main problems with which we have to grapple. He made very accurate comments on our parliamentary system and I support them generally, save as concerns Standing Order 75c, which is quite normal.
I share his view that our first goal should be Canada's development, but I may add that such an objective should include the security and liberty of every Canadian.
My congratulations are also meant for the seconder of the motion, who did very well. He had enough courage to say how high the unemployment rate is in this area of the country. He spoke briefly of the problem of the dairy industry and said that he is far from brushing aside criticisms from farmers against the government dairy policy for 1969-70.
In the Speech from the Throne of the first session we expected the government to talk about agricultural policy.
In last year's Speech from the Throne I had hoped for the announcement of a new farm policy, mainly for changes designed to solve the very serious problem now confronting Canada's industrial milk producers.
I was greatly disappointed in the last session with the way the industrial milk was dealt with. I had hoped that hon. members would have the opportunity to discuss that policy before its application so as to be able to suggest the necessary changes. But alas there again I was greatly disappointed.
On March 31, 1969, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) made known at the very last minute the government dairy policy for 1969-70. It is unfortunate that things are done that way.
The producers were always hoping that we would have the opportunity to discuss this matter in the house, due to the almost general dissatisfaction of the dairy producers caused by a policy that penalizes a number of farm labourers.
Reducing the subsidy from $1.33 to $1.25 per hundredweight resulted in a considerable loss of revenue for the manufactured milk producers. The tax increase on exports to 26 cents per hundredweight, as well as the additional tax of 52 cents per hundredweight on surplus production set by the quota, compared with that of 1968, contributed also to the drop in the farmers' revenues, thus creating more acute problems.
October 28, 1969
In any event, we have been told, rightly maybe, that the reduction of the subsidy and the lowering of the quota, as compared with 1968, were due to a more plentiful production, which resulted in a surplus.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the excess production that we may have, in Canada, is possibly due, I admit, to an increase in production. But another factor has contributed also to this surplus: it is the importation of 188 million pounds of coloured spread and of 47 million pounds of dairy products of all kinds.
These dairy products and this spread have been put on the Canadian market and as the income of the Canadian people has a tendency to decrease, especially the workers' income, I understand why the consumers are inclined to buy cheaper products.
In last year's report, the Economic Council of Canada stated that one Canadian family out of five lives in dire poverty. It would be possible to dispose of a greater quantity of dairy products if the revenue of those who really need them were increased. The amendment moved by my colleague from Portneuf (Mr. Godin), asking the government for a guaranteed minimum income for all Canadians, would bring about an improvement.
I would also invite the government to seriously consider the briefs which have been presented to the standing committee on agriculture by the C.F.U. and the Federated Cooperative of Quebec, when the committee toured the eastern provinces and Ontario.
Those suggestions will probably be examined by the committee, but since time is running short, I would ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) for an early publication of the committee report, in order to find a solution retroactive to April 1, 1969.
It will perhaps be objected that we can only eat our fill. Right, but I will answer that we can only buy according to our purchasing power and when there is only one wage-earner in a family and there are seven, eight or ten months to feed, it is not surprising that the available purchasing power is insufficient.
This is another reason why it would be necessary in Canada to increase indirectly the income of our Canadian families without it having any effect on prices. There are in the country 13 million persons without any income who are dependent on 8 million workers whose income is made up of salaries and profits. One part of the world does not know how to dispose of its production, while the other is destitute. This phenomenon exists in Canada as in other countries.
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert [DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
He had the opportunity to find out during October what Mr. Pearson, former prime Minister of Canada, was asking not only of the Canadian government, but also of other governments, because of the mission that has been entrusted to him. He asked them to investigate the assistance given to the poor countries by the rich ones. In his report, we find the following phrase "Transfer of resources between rich and poor countries".
Canada has an abundance of resources, an abundance of products. I believe that we could afford to increase our assistance to the countries that are really in need. This would be a humanitarian deed which, at the same time, would be of service to Canadian agricultural workers.
My attention was drawn to an article published in L'Action of October 20, 1969. At some function at the United Nations, a former CBC announcer stated, and I quote:
"the real cause of the Nigerian conflict lies in millions of barrels of oil."
and I believe that is right, and I quote further:
"Let us have the courage to admit that no economic interest is worth two million people."
added Mr. Burke who had been invited to speak at the events that took place to celebrate United Nations Day.
The Prince, with head bowed, followed the proceedings in front of a large picture showing a famished Biafran child.
"I ask you to note the expression-
I hope that he was not addressing his question to the Prince but to his audience.
*-on the child's face, this could be your own child, this could be you."
In view of the present situation, I suggest that responsible politicians generally want to tackle the problems facing humanity: poverty and surpluses.
The income of manufactured milk producers has declined in 1969, and we are now coming back to the reasoning of a former federal minister of agriculture who said, in 1965, something extraordinary, as reported in an article entitled "Quebec farmers complain for nothing". I quote:
"Farmers from Quebec and elsewhere are complaining with a full stomach", Mr. Harry Hayes, Minister of Agriculture, indicated yesterday at a press conference. "Those who speak of stagnation are talking through their hats", he categorically stated. The minister applied his remarks both to

October 28. 1969

The Address-Mr. A. Lambert the dairy industry and to agriculture in general. "A Quebec farmer would need, he contended, six dairy cows and two hogs only to net an annual income of $2,400."
Mr. Speaker, the government took the necessary measures to improve the lot of dairy producers and farmers in general. They refused to believe that statement from the minister.
In 1967 also, representations were made by our farm organizations. The situation improved again, and in 1968, it was still much better. I take pleasure in repeating this, because it is true, and I do this to encourage farmers and producers to improve their milk and their herds, in order to meet governments' requirements.
However in 1969 the disaster begins. So I ask myself the following question: Do we really intend to go back to what the minister said in 1965?
In any event it is necessary to face things squarely and to examine the situation seriously. We must recognize that if the province of Quebec has produced the greater volume of industrial milk, losses have been greater there also. Not only have millions of dollars not found their way into the farmers' pockets, but because of the decrease in subsidies, fines and taxes on exports, their income has decreased.
Thus indirectly, without noticing it, the government is supplying with arguments those who are in favour of separatism in Quebec.
Some will say, and rightly so, even if I do not share that opinion, that the federal government is to blame. If we have fewer millions in the province of Quebec, it is again because of the policy worked out in Ottawa, and we are right in wanting to secede.
Mr. Speaker, I know these arguments have a false ring and must be turned down, but, in any event, we have to face the facts.
We sometimes hear too: Those darn farmers, they are never satisfied. The more they get, the more they ask for, and subsidies will have to be cut. If some day they want to get rid of that policy, its phasing out must start now.
Mr. Speaker, the subsidies granted by the government for manufactured milk benefit first and most of all the Canadian consumer. We, manufactured milk producers do not care whether the price of the product is paid entirely by the consumer or if part of it is absorbed by the consumer and the government. The fact remains that the product has its value and the producers are entitled to be

paid for it: this is where the farmers' income comes from.
Because of this policy which should be changed without delay, a great number of farmers have left the farm. There have been auctions by the hundreds. One only has to travel across the eastern provinces to realize the number of farm hands who have left the trade and are now unemployed or exist on welfare.
A very small number have succeeded in landing jobs in industry, in rural centres or in towns, and that has contributed to increase the plague of unemployment. It is for this reason that I urge the government to implement its program of economic expansion and industrial development of rural centres.
In order to decentralize industry, it is not enough to talk about it. Action is called for. And I have found only recently that there are responsible men with drive and the ability to run industries, provided they Eire permitted to breathe, so that their undertaking may prove successful.
The high interest rate, credit restrictions, in short, all kinds of annoyances contribute to discourage those who have initiative and who wish to do something.
In a parish of my constituency, at Saint-Francois, a man had one day the tremendous idea of launching a small industry way out in the country. I went to see it last Saturday and was amazed to realize how this man, whose sons are interested in the expansion of their family undertaking, was successful in building up something fantastic and creating an industry which Americans come to visit and where they place orders. This concern provides employment for our Canadians and, at the same time, a market for Canadian products. There are 65 families earning a living in that industry.
Last summer, the director-this is not even a company-decided to enlarge the plant. After applying to the Economic Development Board in order to obtain benefits offered by the government to those who need them, he received a letter which left him with the hope that he might benefit from grants made in such circumstances. I hope that the problem will be settled but, at any rate, the deal fell through and that man, who could still expand his industry considerably, simply decided to cut the expansion short and even, if it were possible, to sell his business, perhaps to some Americans.
As members of parliament, we ought to take our responsibilities and to see to it that
October 28, 19G9

The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
such measures are really beneficial to rural centres, so that small businesses may develop and provide more jobs for our workers who have given up agriculture and have now to be retrained.
I have before me a table which is an answer to a question I put on the order paper, about the subsidies granted under Bill C-129, in 1968. This is the answer that was given to me: In the province of Quebec, the subsidies granted were of the order of $54 million and the amounts paid out totalled $8 million.
Unfortunately, out of the $8 million, $4.5 million were absorbed by two large corporations and the balance was distributed among small industries.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest we should encourage the development of large corporations, but we should not forget small industries. Besides, we should endeavour to reach an early decision, in order to enable those who have any initiative left, to do something for the development of Canada.
Lately, I read in a newspaper that the Manitoba premier is also his way and wants his province to benefit from industrial development. He is probably using the same arguments as we are. Here is what he said in Montreal:
By keeping for myself the Department of Industry and Commerce, I hope I can give the assurance that we shall keep on encouraging private business to come and settle in our province and to take advantage of the numerous opportunities for investments that are to be found there.
I think that if it is good for the people there to work in this way, it would be equally advisable to do the same in our province and it is high time that this opportunity be given to all those who have initiative and the courage to undertake something and to make a success of it despite the obstacles.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In the Quebec area, one shipyard employed 2,000 workers. I attended a meeting organized by the C.N.T.U., on September 30, in order to meet responsible people in the area, at the municipal as well as the provincial and federal levels. I was surprised to hear that the Lauzon shipyard has jobs for only 800 people. The situation affects some workers in my riding who are now unemployed since they earned their living at the shipyard.
I would like to draw the government's attention to the fact that in 1880, Canada had 7,300 freighters. We then held the fourth place among the countries of the world. In
1969, we had dropped to the twenty-first, because we have only four ships.
If we do not have any ship nor merchant marine, I understand that we do not need any shipyard. However, we should ask ourselves the following question: Do we have the necessary streams for shipping? Do we have goods to be shipped? Do we have workers to build those ships? Do we have shipyards? Have we all what is required to accomplish something? To that, I will answer yes. We can take advantage of the magnificent St. Lawrence river and the Great Lakes. We have access to the seas. Ore, wood, commodities, etc. must be shipped. If it is profitable to ship all those goods in foreign bottoms, it seems that they could be shipped in Canadian bottoms. It would also enable our workers to do their best, because we have specialized workers in those fields.
What is missing to realize all that? The answer is always the same: money! People say that the Creditistes always see a dollar sign. It is true and it must be said. I mentioned all sorts of necessary things, but where is the dollar sign to make all these things work.
I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government-I do not confine myself to criticism, for what is good. I take pleasure in doing so.
They want to tackle the problem of water pollution. It is an excessively serious one. People may not realize it, but those who care for the future, for the health of mankind, have made studies and in their reports have recommended that the governments, at all levels, take the necessary action in order to check this plague.
Unfortunately, farmers are contributing indirectly, and without knowing it, to water pollution, through the use of various fertilizers and chemicals which are carried everywhere by the streams, the rivers, the Great Lakes.
I therefore invite the government to do a little more research on chemical products in order to find a non-chemical way of activating plant production.
I realize that my time is running out. Unless the Chair allows me to finish my speech, and this is why I hurry, I should like to draw the attention of the house to another problem which is crucial in my region: retraining courses for adults.
Every week, I receive numerous phone calls and letters from individuals who are refused by Canada Manpower Centres and are told: We have no room for you, all places rented
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. A. Lambert have been taken and we cannot accommodate any more students.
Mr. Speaker, I am asking the responsible minister to inquire while there is still time- it is still only October-to see if it would not be possible to rent student places in greater number in order to meet the requirements of the people who are not too lazy yet to refuse to go to school. They want to do something. It may perhaps not be 200 per cent beneficial, but at least they should be given the opportunity to believe that they are useful and to become useful in the future, because as we develop industry we will require their services
I have read in the Speech from the Throne that the government intends to reform taxation. A study is contemplated in order to assess taxes in a more equitable manner, and I am for it. I would wish that that study will take two factors into account. Indeed there is an area where, in Canada as elsewhere, it is necessary to unite two things to implement a project. I am thinking of labour and capital. When it comes to taxing labour, it is always more heavily taxed than capital and the proof is in the 1969-70 budget. Indeed labour is taxed at the rate of $4,190 million and capital, that is the big corporations, is taxed at the rate of $2,210 million, a difference of $1,980 million.
When the time comes to reward labour and capital, invariably capital is put ahead of labour. Here is proof. According to a table published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics for the year 1968, personal savings of workers amounted to $4 billion while those of large corporations totalled $8 billion.
In my opinion, it is imperative to study the situation and attempt to find a solution in order to distribute the fiscal load more evenly.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks by saying that there are in Canada very intelligent people capable of great discoveries and great accomplishments in all fields. They are highly qualified managers because they are with it people, people who can do things and initiate reforms. But when it comes to the monetary system, they give up because it is sacrosanct. Nobody wants to touch it, nobody wants to fix it.
Those who claim that major Douglas' proposals for adapting the monetary system to modern realities are illogical, are sometimes people who would have us forget our real economic problems. Their claims serve as
[Mr. Lambert (Bellechasse) .1

a drug to make us forget the great problems of the day.
To my mind, problems should not be glossed over, truth hidden, and the people asked to deprive themselves, to tighten their belt, when we know not what to do with our production, the wealth accumulated by men for men. According to me, this is truly a drug. It is a drug because it is unrealistic.
I therefore support the amendment moved to provide a guaranteed minimum income for all Canadians, because that is physically possible. It will certainly not be likely to make lazy people out of them, no more than those who are wealthy have become lazy. It has been proved that when one is lucky enough to have the money required to undertake something, one works night and day. We are not lazy people.
