speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respectfully offer you my compliments at the outset of this new session. The way you continue to carry out your important functions entitles you to the esteem and the admiration of all hon. members.
I am pleased to congratulate again in this house the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) as well as my good friend the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau). They admirably carried out their important task and their well informed comments are an indication no doubt of the high quality of the debates which will take place in this august chamber.
Mr. Speaker, I would have a great many subjects to discuss today. Some members of the opposition might find it strange that I do not praise the Speech from the Throne but I want to reassure them immediately because I do not dissociate myself from it in any way. This afternoon I had to tape a radio program
October 28, 1969
and my constituents will know Sunday the support I give to the new legislation proposed in the Speech from the Throne.
During the 30 minutes available to me, I will deal in some detail with some of the problems which confront the potato growers in my area. I hope that these comments will seem to my city colleagues mainly, like a refreshing breeze since last year they were compelled to listen to endless debates on wheat, which no doubt will continue for some time yet.
I am going to deal now with potatoes, which is a matter of concern for me and of great interest to a lot of my constituents.
Mr. Speaker, a few weeks before parliament resumed, I had the opportunity to work at harvesting potatoes in my constituency. At that time, schools are closed for two weeks, not only to allow schoolboys and schoolgirls to earn some money in order to buy decent winter clothes, thus alleviating the burden of the family bread-winner, but also because there is a shortage of manpower at harvest time. In spite of the machinery they have now they still have to hire people to work in the fields. Everybody is engaged in the harvesting of potatoes. It is the main concern of the majority of the people for about a month, from September 15 to October 15.
The growing and processing of potatoes, together with the paper and pulp industry are the basis, the structure of the economy in my area.
The slightest fluctuation on the potato market are immediately reflected, on the Sunday collection in rural areas as well as on the volume of business of furniture and car dealers.
The potato industry is a precarious one. Some influences beyond the control of producers are more often than not detrimental to them.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Of course, there is some appearance of a certain prosperity which seems to impress the people visiting our area; however, in many cases, the buildings conceal serious financial problems affecting farmers.
True, Mr. Speaker, the quality of a product is the first factor that influences a buyer. I dealt with the matter in the course of the first session and I do not intend to bring it up again. Nevertheless, I must say that quality control is subject to rules and regulations
The Address-Mr. Corbin made by the federal Department of Agriculture and to their enforcement. In that respect, the accredited fruit, vegetable and potato inspectors responsible for controlling the quality before a product appears on the interprovincial market or the export market, are faced with some difficulties.
Evidently, our potato shippers apprecaite legal restraints no more than our other citizens. Yet, most of them accept such restraints because they result in a product of better quality and, needless to say, in better prices.
But, to be fair, a legal restraint must apply equally to all.
And yet, in the potato industry, as in others, some people sit on the fence, so to speak, in respect of what the law does and does not allow. Thus, some shippers always manage to evade the rules and, consequently, the inspector and the inspection, by means of subtle wiles.
It is a well known fact that 15, 20 or 30 years after the enactment of a law, a person of average intelligence succeeds in finding ways to evade it. It is also admitted that successive amendments to a law, amendments to provide for exceptions, weaken its intrinsic value and make it so flexible that precedents make its implementation impossible.
What precisely makes it difficult to control the quality of table potatoes or of seed-potatoes for export is first of all that a few shippers do not comply with inspection regulations or fail to honour the confidence placed in them by some rules; secondly, the rules now in effect open the door wide to abuses and thirdly, the government austerity program prevents the inspectors from working overtime so that they cannot claim any additional travel expenses in the course of their regular duties.
I already mentioned human weakness as regards potato shippers. I now want to refer to the weakness of the legislation and rules on marketing. Here is what happens to potatoes shipped to another province, Quebec or Ontario, which are our main domestic markets. The law provides that any shipment ought to be inspected before crossing a provincial border. Normally, shipment and inspection take place before six o'clock in the evening during regular working hours.
Sometimes it is absolutely necessary to load a truck rather late in the evening to meet certain terms of a sales contract. I said "in the evening". It is then impossible to have an inspector due to the austerity program because higher officers have instructed their

October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Corbin subordinates not to make any inspection after 5 or 6 o'clock. If they do so, they are not paid any travelling expenses or extra salary.
Inspectors are therefore staying home and some shippers, aware of the difficulty they would have in designating the quality of their potato shipment, take advantage of that to contravene the regulations which encourage them to do so. The shipper can, as a matter of fact, obtain a permit, a release at the inspector's home and then get an authorization from the weighing officer of the highways department to proceed to Quebec.
Of course, potatoes are always subject to an inspection at the point of delivery, be it Gaspe, Montreal, Ottawa or London. However, potatoes are so seldon inspected at the point of delivery, that there might as well not be any inspection. If inspections were stricter, surely, some shipments would be confiscated, but we never hear about any such thing. Thus, low grade potatoes finally reach the large markets, to the prejudice of conscientious growers and the reputation of our product.
I wonder if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) is aware of this practice. I think he would agree with me that the absence of a strict control in the long run can only work against the good standing of our potatoes and give New Brunswick producers a poorer competitive position.
I ignore what is being done in Prince Edward Island or in other provinces in this respect. It remains, however, that most farmers graciously accept compulsory inspection. It is the best guarantee that their product will meet the highest government standards. Our farmers work hard to assure the fine quality of potatoes. They invest annually in the industry they cherish thousands of dollars to buy certified seeds. They take infinite care to control all kinds of contagious diseases.
The harvest is still quite an expensive operation nowadays and as the cost of farm machinery is not decreasing, as we know, profits are finally never guaranteed.
The potato market has experienced disturbing fluctuations during the past four years. This year, we are regaining confidence, because of crop failure in other countries and because apparently, it was not as good as it is usually here.
All this to say that awkward regulations and dishonest shippers can jeopardize the good reputation of New Brunswick potatoes in the province of Quebec and in Ontario as well.

It is necessary to pass more stringent regulations, to abolish those which have become obsolete, or else completely do away with regulations. But then, I think that would mean flirting with disaster.
Nobody, not even the shippers of bad quality potatoes, will lose. On the contrary, all shippers will benefit from the good reputation of a Canada No. 1 product from New Brunswick, and they will get higher prices as an extra bonus.
Another factor which makes it possible to avoid inspection is the allocation by the Department of Agriculture of warehouse numbers. A registered warehouse can ship table potatoes to another province, without inspection at the shipping point, but subject to inspection at the point of delivery. The original aim of this regulation was good, but there is so much abuse-some shippers take this as an excuse to ship goods of inferior quality-that the system of registered warehouses has lost some of its shine, if not all its value.
I do not invent these things and I insist in bringing them to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture.
I had several talks recently with farmers, shippers and federal government inspectors in my region; they all agree that the release permits and the system of registered warehouses must be investigated immediately so as to render justice to farmers and shippers who are careful to abide by all the provisions stipulated in the act in order to market top quality products, something which entails considerable expenses.
Those permits should be cancelled and then the inspectors should be given the tools that they need to do their work properly and completely. They should be paid for their overtime and reimbursed for the expenses incurred by them while carrying out their duties, whether in the day-time, at night or on Saturdays.
A small number of farmers or of potato shippers have obviously no right to endanger the potato market by their dealings or their violations of the regulations. The government has a moral obligation, as long as this act remains in force, to see that it is strictly enforced.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I am under the impression that the Minister of Agriculture is not aware of those problems, perhaps because his high officials themselves are not. If they are, it seems to me that they
October 28, 1969

do not see the disastrous effects of the austerity program, having regard to the quality control program related to potato shipments in a designated area of the Maritimes, which means a lot.
I would not be telling the whole truth if I were to put all the blame on the farmers of my region. I know, from reliable sources, that some Quebec buyers very often buy in our region potato shipments which are never subject to federal inspection.
Naturally, this is mostly done at night. It could also take place during the day as there are never enough inspectors to meet the requirements at certain times.
In this regard I would hardly accept that the following proposal come under the austerity program: that the number of part-time and seasonal inspectors be materially increased to meet the present demand. In normal times, a permanent inspection team would be enough, but when important export contracts are negotiated, there are not enough inspectors to perform the task. Inspection, which also offers the farmer an opportunity to learn, is carried out too quickly in order to look after everyone.
Please note that I am not criticizing the principle nor questioning the merits of the austerity program itself. I am rather in favour of it. I simply question whether this is the right time to apply it to the potato inspection service which is quite essential.
Mr. Speaker, the government and the Minister of Agriculture gave a hand to potato growers last year for the third year in a row. That measure was greatly appreciated and the $600,000 subsidy granted under that program gave some hope to an industry which was beginning to feel the pressures of an overproduction that kept increasing from year to year.
Last year, in the house, we heard a great deal about the problems of wheat producers. I am quite sympathetic to their requests for governmental assistance, believe, me, because there was really a problem there. The assistance program is still and will remain in effect for some time.
The conditions in which New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island potato growers find themselves are strikingly similar to those of western wheat farmers, except that potato growers are far less numerous. The cultivated area is much smaller and the total value of a potato crop will never be comparable to the -wheat harvest of a crop year.
The Address-Mr. Corbin
We should not for all that consider as less important the potato industry, which constitutes the basis of farm activities in the Maritimes provinces and represents, in 1969, a total of many million dollars.
On the national level, the potato's importance is very small but as far as we are concerned in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, things are quite different. And the big difference is that the potato, unlike wheat, is a highly perishable product.
I wonder if the potato grower in the Maritimes, or in Canada, realizes that the potato market is over-saturated, year after year, and that as a result prices barely cover spring investments.
What the potato grower lacks most when planting time comes is a rough idea of the total number of acres that will be planted in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and even out west. Planning should be done in this regard, at the national level.
We also feel the effects of the lack of planning of our neighbours in Maine and other states in the western U.S.A., where huge quantities of potatoes are grown.
None of us have a sure way of forecasting, with any degree of accuracy, what the coming crop will be. Of course, it is difficult to predict, but not impossible. In addition, the first crop forecasts of the federal government are often inaccurate, and when they are revised, more often than not towards the end of December, there is a sudden dip in the price of potatoes on the market.
This means that a better way should be found of assessing the crop, as soon as it comes up, in the fall, so that action might be taken more rapidly and, especially, more accurately, so that the industry will not be dealt an awful blow at the peak of the sales season.
For many years, and even today, the market price the grower gets for his potatoes depends on many factors which often have nothing at all to do with logic.
There is much speculation in that field, and it is true that fortunes have been made or lost through speculation alone.
Still, it seems to me, as it does to an increasing number of potato growers, that the market price should not depend solely on speculation, but should rest to a greater extent on a logical system.

I will give you one example of the highly speculative nature of potato marketing as
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Corbin quoted in the latest issue of Fraser's Potato Newsletter, subtitled "Prince Edward Island's only Publication for Potato People", published by Harry Fraser Hazelbrook in Prince Edward Island. It is a good publication. This passage in particular speaks for itself:
Ontario's potato crop is nearly all under cover, we understand and, as we predicted in earlier letters, it was a very light crop. One prominent Al-liston area grower contacted us this week and advised that the Maritimes could have the eastern Canada potato market tied up this winter, if Maritime growers would only realize their commanding position. This is not an independent opinion either as the Ontario Fruit and Vegetable Growers Association's weekly potato information letter has counselled Ontario growers to "sit back and hold potatoes and let the Maritimes supply the cheap product until they are sold out, then let's move in and take the market".
To say the least, such a state of affairs could be considered by us to be completely unsatisfactory. However, in my opinion it points out quite clearly the need for some kind of controlling body, preferably national in scope, to rationalize the marketing of potatoes throughout the nation, and especially to meet head-on the increasingly severe competition from U.S. producers and European surpluses which slowly but surely are invading some of our more stable and traditional South American markets.
The federal government cannot enter the field of provincial jurisdiction by setting up what would amount to a national potato marketing board without the provinces' consent and co-operation. On the other hand, it would be as a first step the role of the federal government to show leadership in the field by pointing out to the provinces the urgent need for the establishment of such a body and the danger of the collapse of the potato industry generally if yearly surpluses are allowed to continue much longer. I do not know why the application of gentle pressure on the provinces would not lead them to agree to the formation of such a national body, giving it powers with teeth in order to check the degeneration of what was once a flourishing industry.
It is true that the traditional marketing of potatoes is rapidly being overtaken by the marketing of processed products. An announcement was made this summer that McCain Foods of New Brunswick would establish a $5 million potato processing plant in my native city of Grand Falls in my riding. The news was heartily welcomed. It was also announced that the plant would be the first

industrial venture to be considered for subsidy under the new Regional Development Incentives Act. I am confident that under this new act, at least one more processing plant will be established in my riding, thus creating many hundreds of jobs. However, we must realize there is also the danger of the potato market becoming a monopoly of a few. Time does not allow me to develop this idea further but, believe me, it is a matter of growing concern to potato growers throughout New Brunswick.
The processing of potatoes is solving some of our marketing problems, but it will certainly not be the ultimate solution. The traditional way of marketing through brokers may be with us for some time yet, but I am sure it could benefit from more rationalized methods of meeting competition and pricing. I hope our government will take some leadership in this field before potato producers find themselves in a situation similar to that of the western wheat grower.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)

I hope that the present potato selling campaign will have excellent results. Everybody was pleased, for example, with an export contract for 600 wagons of potatoes intended for Chile but first drought had to strike Chile so that we could profit by it.
Potato growing as well as wheat growing cannot and must not rely on agricultural disasters in other countries. I can assure you that the potato grower of my area, at least, is the last man to wish that his activity be subsidized, to the tune of millions of dollars, by the federal government. He would rather leave his farm than accept this.
However, it would be unfortunate to be driven to that because the best potatoes in the world are grown in my constituency.
I am convinced that a little imagination, goodwill and a lot of co-operation between the provinces and the federal government can promote this market on a more solid basis.. This is my present wish.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is expired but I ask for the indulgence of the-house so that I can finish my speech which will last perhaps three more minutes.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I would like to quote from a publication of the now defunct Atlantic Development Board, entitled "The Competitive Position of Maritime Agriculture," published earlier this year in Ottawa. This is a remarkable study of great value. In connection with potato production it is stated very plainly that not only can potato production in the Maritime be sustained at its present level, but there is also room for expansion. I quote:
The potential for expansion for potato production in the Maritimes is related primarily to increases in demand in areas outside the Maritime region. For Maritime producers this increase could come from three sources: population increase in central Canada, a larger share of the domestic market and increased exports. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have virtually the entire seed export market for Canada and if their quality can be maintained their advantage will likely continue. Table stock exports and exports of processed products from Canada also originate mainly in the Maritimes. Maritime producers and processors should be able to capture a large proportion of any export expansion in these products. All of these aspects of the potato market (seed exports, domestic and export table stock markets, and domestic and export markets for processed potatoes) need further study and analysis before the potential for expansion in Maritime potato production can be fully and satisfactorily appraised.
So there it is. Who will tie the bell around the cat's neck, Mr. Speaker? May I humbly suggest that further investigation in this field be carried out by the ADC., the successor of the ADB. I would like to see a more aggressive and permanent sales and promotion campaign undertaken in all countries of our traditional South American market. However, it must be undertaken early in the year. I am under the impression that we missed the boat last year in this respect. So far this year things have improved somewhat.
Potatoes should receive at least a tenth of the attention now accorded wheat in respect of negotiating trade agreements with foreign countries. Canada is but a midget in potato production compared with many European countries, but Europeans know that we have one advantage over their produce-that is quality. With quality we can compete favourably with any country in the world for foreign markets. Right now I believe our handicap is insufficient effort in regard to promotion. If the Minister of Industry, Trade
The Address-Mr. Skoberg and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) can convince me otherwise, so much the better. However, other countries have shipping advantages that we do not have, as well as lower shipping costs and greater proximity to foreign markets. This enables them to more easily dump their yearly surpluses.
No wind is a favourable wind to the sailor who cannot decide which port he is making for. So I say here and now, let this government establish goals. To the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who in my opinion is one of the best captains that boat ever had, I say: Head out for these ports with a full cargo of Canada No. 1 table or seed potatoes. If they originate from New Brunswick so much the better.

Mr. Speaker, I can think of no better way of starting my speech tonight than to refer to the Canadian Commission for UNESCO and an article in its bulletin entitled "Man and his Environment." I believe all of us in the House will agree that we have men, women and children in this country and that we do have an environment. The problem we have not yet solved is how to have a society in which men, women and children can live in a proper environment, with dignity and in tune with the times in which we live. The article to which I referred said that the experts had called attention "to the present fact and future danger of serious pollution, degradation, or outright destruction of the natural environment of which man is a part."
I am sure all of us were pleased that the Throne Speech said pollution control legislation would be introduced in this House. Only time will tell whether that legislation will have teeth. I am also sure we agree that all areas of Canada are polluted. Speaking of my own area, the various streams in the Moose Jaw region have been polluted by people who have made use of natural resources. I wish the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) from Saskatoon-Humboldt were in the House tonight. During the summer he visited the west and spoke at a number of Liberal meetings which were not open to the general public. He told the people there that some of their pollution problems would have to be solved by themselves. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that people as individuals do not pollute our streams. Manufacturing plants must bear the prime responsibility for such pollution and should be held responsible for
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Skoberg correcting the situation. I quote further from the article "Man and his Environment".
The positive aspects of man's control of his environment will be explored to determine the most effective way to achieve a design for living that would encourage the pursuit of beauty and enhance dignity in human relationships.
Some time ago I received from one of my constituents a letter about pollution. I am sure many hon. members remember the television program "The Way It Is", which dealt with a number of cases of pollution. My constituent dealt with the matter much more succinctly than I possibly could. Referring to logging in Algonquin Park, he wrote:
-I wish to stress that all men of vision must condemn this practice. Surely it is the duty of all such men to constantly maintain vigil to see that the few unspoiled areas preserved in our national and provincial parks be passed on unimpaired to future generations of Canadians. Surely a country blessed with the resources of Canada need not infringe on the few wilderness areas set aside for non-commercial roles. Surely the practice of proper timber resource management... of commercial forest areas should ensure that all future generations of Canadians will be guaranteed the enjoyment of exploring and enjoying the unimpaired beauty of Canada's national and provincial parks.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
He continues a little later, referring to the type of strip mining going on in the Koote-nayS-and I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) is well aware of the situation there:
... to restore such strip mining areas to a degree as will eliminate the occurrence of acid mine drainage from polluting our rivers and as well enable reforestation of the area thus avoiding undue erosion as well as making the area of some future value ...
Mr. Speaker, the only purpose in raising this matter now is to assure the minister responsible for pollution control that he will have the utmost support if he will put teeth in the legislation he brings before the House. Unfortunately, I believe it will be a watered-down version, a "voluntary" type legislation, which means very little in this day and age. When the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) was in the west recently he mentioned that the municipalities should be asked to initiate programs supporting the legislation. I have brought this statement to the attention of the municipalities that I have visited recently and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the minister responsible for the legislation will be deluged with letters and information which he will find very useful if he is really concerned about the problem.
[Mr. Skobergl.

I now turn to something in a more serious vein-and I am not suggesting that pollution is not most serious. As one person out in the west said recently, he has two concerns: one is immediate cash in his pocket and the other is survival. He was talking about pollution of our atmosphere and the pollution of our general economic climate. Recently there has come to light the proposed dismissal and firing of many civil servants. The leader of my party has already dealt with this matter. I am sure that we in this House agree that responsible government needs an efficient staff of civil servants. I would like to quote from a speech made some time ago-before I was born, in fact. Lord Dufferin, speaking to the Agricultural and Arts Association in Toronto on September 24, 1878, had this to say, and I think the same holds true today:
The civil service of the country, though not the animating spirit, is the living mechanism through which the body politic moves and breathes and has its being. Upon it depends the rapid and economical conduct of every branch of your affairs and there is nothing about which a nation should be so particular as to secure in such a service independence, zeal, patriotism and integrity.
This government has unilaterally, with very little consideration and very little negotiation with the Public Service Alliance of Canada, implemented changes which should have been brought about by attrition. I supported the comments made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) in this House when he endorsed the Freedman Commission Report which stated that no changes should be made without prior negotiation. It has been suggested that the Prime Minister's magical figure of 10 per cent could be taken care of by attrition in two years' time. This would look after his austerity program. I would ask that the House, and particularly the government, give serious consideration to the matter of attrition, which has of late been accepted in all responsible management and labour negotiations. If the government deliberately releases some senior civil servants it is quite likely that others will leave of their own accord. We will then have the brain drain we hear so much about. This is a deplorable situation.
In the last two days I have had the opportunity to attend the International Labour Organization conference now in session at the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa. I shall also attend it tomorrow. I am sure we all agree with some of the conventions passed at ILO conferences throughout the years, although they
October 28, 1969
cannot be ratified by the government of Canada because of the provisions of the British North America Act. When we realize that the various provincial governments also have to agree to these conventions, we know why it is difficult to actively participate in the ILO and why very few of the conventions have been passed.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that once again we are getting into a situation where the government of Canada is reversing its stand. Instead of trying to achieve a strong central government, the trend is to decentralize and give the provinces much more power. It has been said that we in Canada believe in strong central government, whereas in the United States of America the states have strong central power. It seems that the United States is trying to achieve a strong central government with less power in the states, whereas Canada is deliberately moving in the direction of more power vested in the provinces and less power to the federal government.
Speaking now for myself and not for my party, Mr. Speaker, I say that the people of Canada are fed up with our educational system wherein people moving through mobility programs from province to province results in children being educated under a number of different educational programs. The armed forces are in the situation where their children may have to experience different educational programs because the individual provinces cannot get together and adopt a uniform system of education. This situation, again, exists because of the British North America Act. If a government is not prepared to accept responsibility, nothing is easier than to blame everything on the B.N.A. Act rather than trying to make the necessary changes to the act.
Of one thing I am positive, Mr. Speaker- that the people of Canada from coast to coast believe in one nation. Sometimes it seems that the government is trying to divide this country by saying that the provinces must be given unilateral authority in certain affairs. I do not believe this authority should be given to them. This may be another situation wherein many legal brains in the country are making a fortune at the expense of the individual, and I say that with due deference, Mr. Speaker.
I would now like to turn to a situation that has come to light in the House and this is in regard to Phillips Cables Limited. This matter has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. 221
The Address-Mr. Skoberg Pepin) on many, many occasions. It is a great disservice for the government to suggest that the company has to look after itself and find its own markets for copper; and it seems ridiculous that Phillips should have to buy Canadian copper through a British firm, the London Metal Exchange, when the copper never leaves Canada, just to comply with the regulations. I know that many people in this House and many editorial writers regard our party as one that believes in the nationalization of all industry. Many in our party believe that if we have regulations to control industry it does not matter whether that industry is foreign or Canadian owned. Phillips Cables represent a Canadian industry that could go out of business today because the government is not prepared to pass regulations which would enable it to operate most successfully.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The government is not prepared to pass regulations which would ensure that the Phillips Cables Limited have adequate supplies of copper to keep it in business. I am expressing not only the point of view of labour but that of management when I say this. This government will stand forever condemned if Phillips Cables are forced out of business because they cannot obtain enough copper. The government cannot use the excuse that the strike is causing difficulty. Many years ago this company attempted to obtain copper from another company which will not now deliver to it. The company had to pay more for copper coming via the London exchange even though the copper was coming from Canada.
I am also disturbed about the freeze applied to non-competitive freight rates in the Atlantic region. In a news article emanating from the Department of Agriculture, the minister said-and I hope he is listening-that beyond doubt the adjustments being made will also correct some inequitable situations which now exist between rate zones, and that specific changes in rates will be announced later by the Canadian Livestock Feed Board. The import of those words is that once again those who are most concerned about the matter will be left in a state of confusion. The news release dated October 16 went on to say:
The increase in demand for Western feed grains has been due primarily to poorer oat and corn crops in Ontario and a more attractive price relationship for feed grains for Western Canada compared to U.S. corn than has prevailed in the past.
I ask the minister, whom are we really trying to protect? Are we protecting our own

The Address-Mr. Skoberg
With regard to the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Speaker, too many people in responsible positions in Canada are deliberately trying to undermine the Wheat Board. I strongly believe that the Canadian Wheat Board can do the job, if given the proper tools. Too often in the past this government and its cabinet have not given the Canadian Wheat Board the tools with which to do the job. I am sure those who remember the loss of a barley sale a year or two ago realize that if the Canadian Wheat Board had been in a bargaining position it may not have occurred. What disturbs me is that international brokerage firms are involved in the marketing and manipulation of our grain. I can only think this is being done in order to get back to the old hatchet system of the open market and to do away with the Wheat Board. In this way more people would become millionaires.
I am sure the minister has looked fully into the situation at the port of Churchill. I am certain this matter has been dealt with in this House. Many hon. members know Mr. Gray, the Secretary-Treasurer of the Hudson Bay Route Association, and agree that we should extend the insurance which is provided there. He indicated that we could increase the sale of these grains through Churchill if the port was allowed a more open season. There is no ice at this time at the port of Churchill, yet the season is closed. This question should be looked into. I hope this has already been done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is customary during the debate on the Speech from the Throne to extend congratulations to all those who have been recognized in a special way since parliament last met-those who have been promoted within the cabinet and so forth-and also to extend congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address. This has been done already by many speakers in the course of the debate and all I intend to add to this traditional aspect of our proceedings is that I heartily endorse those sentiments.
This is not the first debate on the Address in which I have taken part. As a matter of fact, as I look across to my right at the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) I am reminded that it is about 19 years since we were first exposed to the mysteries of this Parliament of Canada; since we arrived on Parliament Hill to conquer new worlds and change the destiny of the nation. I am sure that is the sentiment of a good many members when they first arrive in parliament.
Looking back over that period of Canadian history one realizes that there have been many changes. Some have been for the better and others have been for the worse. I note that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his contribution to the debate on Friday last summed up his remarks by saying, in effect, that it was the government's intention to direct the processes of change in such a way as to ensure they would redound to the general good of Canada. I have the exact words before me as reported on page 43 of Hansard. The Prime Minister said:
We intend in the future as in the past to be the voice of change; we shall not forsake our role as advocate of the great mainstream of Canadians and we intend to listen, to understand, to respond and to lead.
Over the past 19 years I have heard many speeches, as you can well imagine, Mr. Speaker, and I have learned to take many of the
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale sentiments expressed in this chamber with the proverbial grain of salt. I have become somewhat less idealistic than I was when I first came here, and I have concluded that the best way to interpret the earnest of the desire of any administration is not necessarily to draw conclusions from the words which are spoken but to watch the policies of the particular administration or political leader concerned for proof of action in the best interests of Canada.
Tonight I want to deal briefly with some of the changes which have taken place in recent years and which I feel are not in the best interests of this institution of parliament nor in the best interests of the unfolding development of Canada as a nation from sea to sea. I like the sentiment expressed by the Prime Minister in some exalted words at the conclusion of his speech. He said this institution of parliament was designed to resolve differences to which he had referred, and I agree heartily with that proposition. Unfortunately, fundamental changes are taking place in this institution, changes which I feel go in a direction completely opposite to the sentiment expressed by the Prime Minister in his contribution to the debate the other afternoon. Maybe in considering this question of change we have arrived at a point where the change is so fundamental that it is almost as profound as during a period such as the Reformation, which changed the basic perspectives of the society of that time.
Values are changing in the world in which we live today. As the old preacher in the book "Green Pastures" expressed it: "Everything not nailed down am coming loose." We are faced with all the problems generated by a fundamental change in values in the direction of relativism of the new morality, and of tensions created by the advent of the permissive society which are having such a disastrous influence on our basic social institutions, be they the family, the institutions of education or even those of parliamentary democracy. It is the virus of this profound change- perhaps I should use the word "poison"- which is biting deep into the body politic. As has been forcibly brought to our attention, this is reflected particularly in the younger generation of Canadians who were born into the nuclear age, who have been programmed into the computer age and who, more recently, were skyrocketed into the space age. In these circumstances it is not hard to understand why there is confusion, as is made

226	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale manifest in some of the activities which have come to public attention, to the attention of the government and to the attention of all members of the House in recent weeks. I quote, for example, what has occurred with respect to the government's charges against the Company of Young Canadians, the group which was established by legislative decree of this House just a few years ago to be a vehicle whereby young Canadians could participate on a voluntary basis in giving guidance amid the profound social changes which have been affecting Canada so seriously.
I could refer also to the disturbances in our universities which have become the occasion of almost daily headlines in our newspapers and which certainly have been reported prominently by that great public organ of information the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which has itself been facing certain difficulties as a result of the deep-seated process of change which has been going on.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The Prime Minister has responded to these indices of confusion and disorganization in Canadian society and, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said so effectively the other day, has engaged in verbal over-kill in order to make the point that he wanted to make at that time. The situation could be expressed in another way: He was, perhaps, using a baseball bat to kill a flea. In other words, Mr. Speaker, his was a sudden, almost emotional, response to a very delicate situation.
Since the statements of the Queen's first minister in Canada have a profound influence right across the country in view of the prestige of that office, if we are not careful, Mr. Speaker, this sort of thing could result in incipient McCarthyism and witch-hunting which, of course, is not a reasonable approach to the problem of reflecting serious social change. Indeed, it has now reached the point where it is attempting to tear at the very foundations of national unity.
One problem in this House of Commons that does not change from year to year is the basic consideration given to policies that are enunciated and brought forward by government, supported by this parliament, which are designed to bring together Canadians of all ethnic origins from sea to sea in what we like to refer to as national unity. The problem of national unity in a country like Canada becomes more difficult to deal with in periods

DEBATES	October 28, 1969
of rapid change, and we are passing through such a period at the present time.
In another statement that the Prime Minister made recently he said he had solved the problem of national unity, and that in another five years he would perhaps be able to move off the political stage. Having listened to hon. members from all parts of Canada in the course of this debate outlining the economic problem that are facing various sections of the country, it would seem to me that a statement of that kind indicates that the right hon. gentleman is very much out of tune with the prevailing mood and spirit of the nation. Never was there a time when there was more restlessness and confusion in the Canadian body politic.
In recent years that there has been a tendency to concentrate upon the issues that separate us rather than upon those that bring us together. The Prime Minister has this exasperating habit of heading in two opposite directions at the same time, and this makes it very difficult for the Canadian people, who are part of the Canadian mosaic, to understand exactly where the Prime Minister is going. It is almost like riding into the eye of a hurricane. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the problem of national unity becomes increasingly difficult during periods of social change. It therefore behooves all of us, in our observations on the subject, to underline and support some of the fundamental institutions which have been the unifying forces in Canada since the beginning of this nation.
For example, I do not think it is helpful at this time constantly to downgrade and erode such a fundamental institution as the monarchy. I do not want to dwell on this theme at any great length, but even in the official references in the documents of Canada we have had it underscored that the role of the monarchy as a symbolic, unifying force in this nation has been downgraded and eroded. The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), in a speech that he made during a visit to London last summer, indicated that Canada will inevitably become a republic. Well, now, that is his belief and his sentiment. For myself I do not think there is anything inevitable about a process of that kind. Actually, the institution of constitutional monarchy has been one of the main sources and symbols of Canadian unity down through the years. Indeed, it has made possible our movement forward as a nation in the midst of all kinds of divisive and centrifugal forces in the Canadian body politic.
October 28, 1969	COMMONS
Another very important example of this technique of moving in two ways at the same time, of downgrading an institution merely because it is traditional and of long standing, is this: At the other end of the scale we find spokesmen for the government, from the Prime Minister down, moving toward a policy of narrow nationalism in recent announcements of changes in defence policy. In the sort of world in which we live, one in which the impact of change is even more profound on the international scene than on the domestic scene, this has caused a spirit of pessimism to prevail at the United Nations. It has also caused the former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, to state that the affluent nations must be more generous in their support of the underdeveloped nations. I think that any institution that has achieved progress in bringing together a consort of nations as a meaningful international body should be supported with increased enthusiasm by the government of Canada. Regrettably, government spokesmen in recent months have seen fit to downgrade NATO.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization was moulded from the challenge of international Communism which arose in the latter 1950's. We in Canada gave until recent times our wholehearted support to this organization. It was regarded, in the first instance, as a co-operative form of military defence on the part of Atlantic nations against the threat of external subversive influences. But it was more than a military force; it was also the nucleus of a political entity.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
It was devoutly hoped it would become the nucleus of a significant political force which might even move forward to become the pioneering experiment in some form of international federalism. Many members of this House have had the opportunity to attend NATO Parliamentary Association meetings. There has always been there great enthusiasm and support for the ultimate objectives of the NATO Parliamentary Association becoming a useful forum that would see the North Atlantic communities grow closer together in the beginning of a new total international co-operation which is urgently needed in the sort of jungle situation which prevails in the dealings between governments at the present time. If we downgrade our military contribution to NATO it
DEBATES	227
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale means that our voice in the political deliberations of that important body will be equally downgraded.
I was overseas this summer for a couple of weeks and was shocked to see the rapid decrease, almost to the vanishing point, of the prestige of Canada in such countries as West Germany, the United Kingdom, Belgium and all the other countries which are playing a vital role in the promotion of the NATO ideal both military and political. We have unilaterally, without consultation with members of this House and certainly ignoring the recommendations of the comprehensive study made by the External Affairs Committee, withdrawn our strong support for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
This is just one example. Many others could be quoted. Perhaps the main criticism I should like to make is that much of this has been done without parliamentary approval. In fact, there has been a move in the opposite direction. Many of the announcements are made outside this House when parliament is in recess. It would almost appear to be a deliberate device to avoid criticism. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister's version of participatory democracy seems to be to appeal directly to public opinion rather than the slower and more difficult process of parliamentary discussion. I believe that one thing in this process of change which has brought about so much confusion in the nation has been the tendency of the government to an increasing extent to downgrade the principle of responsible government which is absolutely essential if parliament is to continue to play the unifying role that the Prime Minister mentioned in his speech when he said this institution of parliament is designed to resolve the differences that are wracking the Canadian community at the moment.
These topics have been referred to many times. I could talk about the roster system whereby ministers show their lack of respect for the principle of responsibility by indicating they feel there are more important duties to attend to in their ministerial responsibilities than listening to hon. members in this House. The tendency of ministers to make statements outside the chamber undercuts the elected representatives on the government and opposition sides of the House. There would appear to be a tendency to govern through the mass media. In this way there is instant communication with instant solutions for all the problems which change almost as
October 28, 1969

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale quickly as the kaleidoscopic images on television. There would appear to be the assumption of a presidential role without the checks and balances of the presidential system. Announcements are made at press conferences rather than in this chamber, particularly on the eve of the opening of parliament. The distinguished parliamentary correspondent, Charles Lynch, refered to this in a recent article when he said:
In their press conferences, few American presidents have ever covered ground as sweeping as Mr. Trudeau did yesterday-telling off France, Quebec separatists, the Company of Young Canadians in rapid-fire order, plus recognizing the Vatican.
He enlarged his cabinet-already the largest in Canadian history-by adding a wheat minister and an assistant finance minister, and said the cabinet might grow even bigger.
The growth of the power of the executive is one of the disturbing features I have noticed take place surreptitiously and constantly in the 19 years I have been in this chamber. If the Prime Minister, when he refers to the process of change and the necessity of consulting the institution of parliament in resolving differences, really means this there must be more than words; there must be action. This action must be vastly different from the action and the attitude which has prevailed in the executive branch of this government since it assumed office just over a year ago.
Parliament is no longer the sounding board of the process of government in Canada. Some people say that parliament is dead, that this House is dead and that there is no interest and no confrontation in debate across the chamber. It is suggested that as a consequence members stay away in droves. The high court of public opinion, the raison d'etre of this institution, tends to become a legislative treadmill. There is nothing that reveals the real intent of this government in the House of Commons more clearly than its insistence on Bill C-75 in the dogdays of the past session last July.
Another problem that relates very closely to this whole difficulty of maintaining national unity in a situation of growing diversity is the necessity to deal with the continuing problems, in fact the growing problems, of regional disparity. Important as parliament is as a sounding board of public opinion, we will not really come to grips with the problems of Canadian nationhood until we deal in concrete terms with specific economic problems.
One of the few specifics mentioned by the Prime Minister during that confused election

of 1968 was the necessity of dealing with regional disparity and bringing about a more equitable economic situation in the various parts of Canada. Unfortunately, in the changing circumstances the poor have become poorer and the rich have become richer. I am referring not only to individuals but to the underdeveloped parts of Canada. There is lack of diversification in the economy because of the tendency for political power as well as economic development to concentrate in the two big central provinces. I believe it should be mentioned that at the present time there are movements both in the far eastern part of Canada and in western Canada. Discussions are going on with a view to making a united appeal to Ottawa to break up the core of economic power in the golden triangle to which reference is often made.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
On looking at the Speech from the Throne I agree with other hon. members who have referred to its lack of specific policies and its generalities in dealing with the great economic issues of Canada. It almost seems that the present government, as was said by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent in reference to the lack of interest of governments over the years in the development of the north, is dealing with the problems of the extremities of Canada, both east and west, in a state of absentmindedness. It appears as if the present government regards east and west as colonies to be placated but not to be provided with the economic programs that are needed if we are to really deal with one of the major difficulties of national unity, that is, regional disparity.
I could point out many examples of this kind, but in view of the shortness of time I would just mention in passing-I see that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier) dealt with the subject the other day- that an important event is to be celebrated both in Manitoba and in the Northwest Territories next year when both these parts of Canada will be celebrating their centennial. This underlines the fact that when Manitoba was first carved out of the Northwest Territories in 1870 and when the Northwest Territories as a whole became a part of the Canadian federation, a new dimension was added to the Canadian community which has added a positive and dynamic force to what we in western Canada call the Canadian mosaic. What has happened in western Canada is that

Thank you for your generosity, Mr. Speaker, and also I thank hon. members. I would like to have dealt with specific problems, such as the problem of the agricultural community in western Canada. Many western spokesmen have brought this difficulty to the attention of the House, and if the Prime Minister and his ministers are really listening, I am sure they will have the basis of policies which if applied to solving the difficulty will make a major contribution in dealing with what has become a major economic crisis.
The crisis has now been recognized in the appointment of a special minister to deal with wheat. I am sure that we will see some solutions coming out of this particular comer of the cabinet. The minister is a westerner; he understands the difficulties and certainly he has had enough advice to enable him to deal with them.
There is only one further contribution that I would like to make in offering advice, that is to underscore the fact that salesmanship is the real solution to the problem of wheat which has become a glut rather than a benefit to the Canadian economy generally. The farmers have already put forward a suggestion which were it adopted by the government would, I am sure, accelerate the sale of the surplus grain that is piling up in the Trudeau bins as the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) referred to them, and it would not cost the public treasury a penny.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has already been approached about this matter. The farmers want to set up a farmer-financed sales agency to get out and sell grain aggressively so as to get beyond the international cartels that have no particular interest in selling Canadian wheat. They would finance it out of a small deduction from each bushel of grain. It would be something similar to the United States export marketing agency which 21362-16
has recently been set up to deal with their similar problem of surplus agricultural products.
I will not transgress further on the time of the House, but by way of summary I will go back to my opening remarks and say that I agree heartily with the Prime Minister when he says that the fundamental problems of Canada today have been aggravated, if not precipitated, by the processes of change that are striking at the very foundation not only of Canadian society but of the world community. Change can be either positive or negative. It does not necessarily bring about a renaissance in national and international life. There must be positive leadership and there must be concrete programs if a just society is to be established in fact as well as in name. It must be based not on words but on action. This is the major criticism of the Speech from the Throne and it is the major criticism of the government. The words are fine, the music is pleasant, but we seem to be dancing in circles. Let us match action with policies and programs to deal with some of the fundamental difficulties to which I have referred briefly and to which reference has been made by other hon. members. Especially let us stop the erosion of the institution of parliament so that members, instead of becoming ciphers and nonentities or, as the Prime Minister himself said in the final days of the last acrimonious session, absolutely useless in dealing with the affairs of the nation can contribute to this much publicized just society.	,|
I say to the Prime Minister: Give us a chance. Listen to the advice. I am sure that we shall meet in a positive way the challenge of change rather than create greater disunity and division in the Canadian nation, which has been the case during the first few months of this administration's life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I shall have the pleasure of closing off this enjoyable day. First I want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I expected those hon. members to make laudatory remarks. People will read their remarks and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has taken notice of them.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Of course, they expect to be lauded and complimented. I have listened to all the other speeches, especially those from backbenchers, and I found them very interesting. Indeed, I

October 28, 1989
The Address-Mr. Otto thought that some of them under the guise of flattery were rather critical of the government, I think that is a good thing. From my experience I would like to tell backbenchers that if they are going to be critical of the government the safest place to do it is right here in the House of Commons. Do not do it in the press because then your criticism will get down to the ministers and to the Prime Minister and you will be chastised. Do not do it in letters to your constituents. Do it here in this House where you are absolutely safe. Certainly there are ministers who attend in this house but they very seldom pay attention to speakers; they are busy writing letters so the backbencher can say what he likes. Further, all the members of the Press Gallery leave the chamber right after the question period. For most of the rest of the time there is only one gentleman sitting in the Press Gallery. This has been my experience over seven years. There are two sitting there now, and that is rather usual. I strongly suspect that one of the gentlemen to whom I refer is not even a reporter; I suspect he is a hired man put there to make it appear that the press is represented in this House.
As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) said, it is sad that this House is no longer an effective House, an effective organ. It is a fact that the parliamentary system does not completely suit this form of government or this country. Most of the time we talk at each other rather than to each other; then the parliamentary secretaries talk to the ministers, the ministers talk to the deputy ministers, the deputy ministers to the establishment, and the establishment talks to God. Nobody really cares what we are saying here. Therefore I repeat my advice to new members. In the seven years that I have been critical of the government not once have I been chastised for being critical of it here in this chamber.
When I approached the bar of the other place to hear the Speech from the Throne I of course could not hear very well because there was no loud speaker system. However, I did catch a couple of words with which I was very pleased.

Anyway, the words I thought I heard were that we were going to have a Canadian research centre or corporation. This has been talked about for many years. It is
[Mr. Otto.)
something we should have, to advise our government. We should have a comprehensive research organization which will at least diagnose our problems carefully and accurately and provide a base upon which the government can act. Unfortunately, when I read the Speech from the Throne I saw it referred to a Canadian international research centre which is to give advice on our contributions to the newly developing nations. Of course, that will be a good thing also. I have no criticism of it, because in many cases aid given by both the United States and Canada has not necessarily been used to the best advantage.
I recall that some years ago in Turkey I saw a brand new road that had been built with American money, a road which sort of went from corner to corner. It started nowhere and ended nowhere, but certainly took in a great number of zigzags. When I inquired why it served no particular purpose I found that certain members of the government had houses or land in various places and the road went through each of those places. Indeed, a great deal of Canadian money has also gone the wrong way. Therefore if this proposed centre is a good one it will serve a useful purpose. However, it seems to me that we in Canada need such an organization-a "think tank" as it was once called. Last year the Prime Minister said he was in favour of such an organization. I think the quicker it is established the better it will be.
I jotted down some of the points that I thought should concern a Canadian research centre if such is formed. It should not merely be concerned with research for marketing or for government. It should be a composite research project. At present we have research branches in various departments of government. This is something quite new; there were none eight years ago. But these branches do not talk to each other. The agricultural research branch feeds advice to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), and other branches advise the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). Each one is on a different tack. We cannot function in this day and age without a composite basis, a carefully packaged research concept that will encompass all departments and work in conjunction with them. This is not something new.
In 1951 the Japanese government formed the Japanese Trade Research Organization for Japanese industry, commonly known as Jetro.
